subtopic: CHICAGO DIVERSION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CHICAGO DIVERSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 8 the hon. member for Rosedale asked:
Would the Prime Minister tell us the attitude of the Canadian government toward the legislation recently passed in the United States House of Representatives in regard to the diversion of water from the great lakes at Chicago?
I replied, after dealing with one or two matters of history, and said:
-we are paying the closest attention to this matter, at the same time not wishing to do anything that would in any way cause a situation to arise which might not be beneficial.
I now wish to bring the house up to date on this subject. When I last spoke on April 8 I stated what the fact was, that the government was giving careful consideration, and since then has given further consideration to the most effective manner of making known Canada's opposition to the bill which, as I said a moment ago, has passed the House of Representatives and is now before the Senate committee on public works. A note registering the reasons for Canada's objection was delivered on April 9, and with the leave of the house I ask permission to table it so that it might possibly appear in Votes and Proceedings. I am not going to read the entire note, but just two particular paragraphs thereof to indicate the general tenor and attitude of the government in this regard. In the third paragraph the following appears:
Every diversion of water from the great lakes watershed at Chicago inevitably decreases the volume of water remaining in the basin for all purposes. The government of Canada is opposed to any action which will have the effect of reducing the volume of water in the great lakes basin. Careful inquiry has failed to reveal any sources of water in Canada which could be added to the present supplies of the basin to compensate for further withdrawals in the U.S.A. The government of Canada considers that many agreements and understandings between the U.S.A. and Canada would be broken if unilateral action were taken to
divert additional water from the great lakes watershed at Chicago and directs attention to provision of two treaties in particular.
The first is the boundary waters treaty of 1909 and the second is the Niagara treaty of 1950.
The general summation of the attitude of the government in this regard is contained in the last two pertinent paragraphs:
Because of the importance attached by the U.S.A. and Canada to the honouring of international undertakings in letter and in spirit, the government of Canada views with serious concern any possible impairment of agreements and undertakings relating to the great lakes basin. Furthermore, the alarms created by repeated proposals for diversion which inevitably disturb the people and industry of Canada are a source of profound irritation to the relations between our two countries which we can ill afford.
I am instructed, therefore, to express the hope of the government of Canada that the U.S.A. will view this matter with equal concern and will be able to give satisfactory assurances that unilateral action will not be taken which would imperil the present regime of the waters in the great lakes basin and the status of the agreements and understandings to which I have referred.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, April 15, consideration of the motion of Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Benidickson, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Regier.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to have the opportunity to speak when there are at least more than the corporal's guard present who will be here tonight when the hockey game is on. One of the points brought up by the hon. member for Hull interested me very much. I do not quite see its relevance to the budget, but he did make some remarks about the position labour should take so far as political action is concerned, and he pointed to the United States situation as a wonderful example of how labour can do very well without taking direct political action.
I should like to suggest to the hon. member, having in mind the whole attitude toward American labour unions and American business, that he cannot have it both ways. Surely any member of the house can recognize that the United States system is so different from ours that political pressure by any lobbying group can be exerted on individual members of the House of Representatives and Senate, who are not welded together in a party unit as is the case in this country. Therefore the United States experience is completely different, and there is much more compulsion toward labour taking political action in this nation than there is in the United States. I am not saying that is complete justification for it, but it is certainly an argument.
On the other hand we are always having the United States example of labour not taking political action held up to us, while at the same time these very same people, and I would not rule out the hon. member for Hull, are the ones who say that we will rue

The Budget-Mr. Fisher the day that we hooked up with international unions. They say it is a terrible thing that Canadian unions should be tied up with United States unions. As a matter of fact over 70 per cent of Canadian unions have American affiliation of some kind or other. It seems to me that you cannot have it both ways. If you are going to argue that the one thing is bad, then surely you cannot argue that the other is bad.
I should like to make another point in that regard. You also have to look at the fact that most of our large economic organizations have a very direct relationship with United States companies. Quite often they are subsidiaries. That is one of the logical points with respect to the international union pattern, because economies within specific industries have a direct relationship. Yet we have this kind of nonsense that is all part of the "clobber labour" picture that seems to be so popular at this time, and if you do not want to stress the other side then at least in fairness this point should be looked at.
I was very interested to notice today in the Montreal Gazette the annual report of the St. Lawrence Corporation containing some very striking comment by the president, Mr. Percy M. Fox. Mr. Fox is a gentleman who got a load off his chest only a couple of months ago about this terrible situation of United States union domination in Canada and how it was the ruination of the country. The interesting thing to me is that amongst the directors of the St. Lawrence Corporation there are several Americans, and there are strong indications that United States capital plays a very large part in this company.
Furthermore, Mr. Fox made the standard insinuation that with this union domination there is no democracy in unions any more. Let us look at the picture with respect to corporations and see how much democracy there is there. There have been a number of recent examples of very small shareholders trying to bring their points of view before corporations. There was one recently involving the Canadian General Electric Company. If you are going to stress democracy in the one case, why is it not stressed in the other?
The point I want to make in connection with this call for democracy has some relationship to a political point. There was an interesting article in the Toronto Star the other day by Mr. John Bird on whether we have a one-man government. I do not entirely agree with all the points he made, but he presented a very challenging point of view that the government that we have today is a one-man government. Certainly my impression from talking to Conservative members

of parliament is that the Prime Minister is very much in control. There is nothing wrong with that. I think we accept that as part of the situation. On this very point I should like to refer to an editorial in the magazine The Reporter for April 2, 1959, where I find the following:
Quite a number of elected politicians still find it difficult to acknowledge the leaders of organized labour as politicians from another realm. We have heard ad nauseam in the halls of congress that union members should incessantly and massively participate in all the major decisions on union affairs and spend their free time watching over their elected representatives. Respectfully, one can ask our congressmen how they would like to have their constituents massively breathing down their necks.
I should like to suggest that the Prime Minister does not have his constituents or the members of parliament who support him in the house massively breathing down his neck at all times, from a democratic point of view. Surely you have to recognize that a union is the kind of organization in which the executive, when elected, has to be given responsibility, especially in the interim periods between elections. Therefore it seems to me that the howl or cry that unions are undemocratic organizations is based upon a misconception of how a union has to carry out its task. If the union executive has to turn around every time any kind of decision is to be made and call a mass membership meeting, I can only suggest that the union would be in a very difficult position, just as difficult a position as if the Prime Minister had to go to the country every time a major decision in politics was to be made.
I think this is a point that really needs to be made and emphasized, because it is all part of the unfair damnation of the labour movement that seems to be so popular in Canada at the present time and especially, I am sorry to say, quite often within the House of Commons.
One of the other points in connection with labour that the hon. member for Hull made was a warning of the danger of getting tied up with the C.C.F. with respect to the idea of forming a new party. I think any fair-minded member in this house will recognize that if there is any possible way in which you can get people discussing politics under almost any auspices in this country, you are achieving something; you are carrying out some kind of educational pattern. I think all hon. members are aware of the apathy that we had. Whether or not this new party movement is successful-I happen to have my hunch there, and it is probably different from the rest-surely it is going to be a fairly large achievement if it presents a challenge to the labour movement, to the

people connected with the labour movement and other citizens who may be interested in it. Surely one result will be an increase in political interest and in the whole tempo of political events. I insist that that is very good, because I feel that one of the reasons we now have perhaps less understanding in our country of the responsibilities of government is because of this apathy, disinterest and the increasing tendency for people to shrug off any mature responsibility toward political events.
There is one other point I should like to make to these people who are taking this interest in the new party. The assumption within this House of Commons always seems to be that this is going to be strictly a labour deal. I should like to remind hon. members, as an example, that the majority of the members in this particular group in the House of Commons have no direct connection with labour, have not come up through any labour organization or labour movement. We happen to be rather proud to some of the achievements of the C.C.F. in a democratic way. The C.C.F., whatever its efforts, has managed to develop a fairly large membership, and that membership has never been based upon any great union strength. I think the government members from Saskatchewan will acknowledge that.
I believe it is complete nonsense to say that out of this development that may be coming you are going to get a political party that is going to be completely dominated by labour. I should like to assure the members who have this interest that within the C.C.F. movement itself there is enough concern, enough interest, in this particular point of view to see that we do not develop a political party that is in any labour leader's pocket. I do not mean by that last remark that I have anything against labour leaders; it is just not going to be that type of political party.
I feel that one of the points made by Mr. Fox in his annual report has a definite bearing upon the budget in a general way, and concerns something for which I have been looking in this House of Commons. I refer to the genuine free enterprisers who belong to these other two majority parties. Mr. Fox says:
Politicians still bet on voters being foolish enough to think that welfarism means something for free, that higher taxes and bigger spending don't matter as long as the hand-outs keep coming. And the politicians still seem right about some people, for there are some who try to think that a government is coping with inflation when it taxes more even though it shows no attempt to spend less.
The Budget-Mr. Fisher
It seems to me this is a direct comment upon the budget presented by the Minister of Finance. Mr. Fox goes on to say:
We cannot look to politicians or any political party to halt the spreading of indiscriminate welfarism. The aim of politicians is to win elections.
This affects all of us. The Minister of National Revenue was very candid the other day in suggesting that there is a lot of difference winning elections and carrying out a program. Mr. Fox goes on:
They tell themselves that the people ask for welfarism: that it will continue to catch votes. Therefore, whether they think it good or bad, political party strategists will go on offering more and more of it until the people themselves stop them. In over 30 years we have had no sign of statesmanship in Canada to let us hope for anything different.
Well, that is a very bleak picture. I think one of the great disappointments to me, as one interested in political ideas and the fact that there should be some sharp division of ideas, is that I have not been able to recognize in that monster party that flows around the sides of this chamber any clear-cut exposition of what I thought they were directly connected with, that is free enterprise, private enterprise and all the rest. I have expressed this opinion before. We find it quite simple, in many cases, to cast our votes for most of the measures that are brought in here. This, if I correctly interpret it, indicates that we have a sprawling, middle of the road party that is away over on the left. Perhaps this is fine and perhaps it will keep members in for a long time, but it makes it very difficult to find any clear-cut political opposition. It is obviously making it difficult for the Liberal party.

speechtext:
I have been asked, did they? Oh, yes, they did.
The difficulty of a definite position here, in so far as a group or a party that feels it is a socialist party is concerned, is simply that so many of the ideas of democratic socialism have permeated right through this chamber that we have difficulty marking out a clear-cut position. This is one of the things we attempt to do, and we will try to do to a greater extent. I know someone made a scornful reference to our amendment as being full of time worn phrases such as "the effect of social and economic planning". I admit that the time-worn phrase "social and economic planning" is not good enough. Of course an amendment does impose on you some limitation in spelling out what you suggest, but certainly our hope is in the future, and certainly our plan will have to be, to spell out in much greater detail both the steps in a welfare direction and the steps in so far as planning is concerned, especially economic planning.
On that last point there is still considerable confusion amongst what I call the less thoughtful people in this country-I will not say they are reactionary-about just what the term "socialism" means. I know that quite often, especially by United States writers, it is taken to be a blanket political program of complete nationalization. One of the points put up was that we did get into the amendment the idea of a capital gains tax. The suggestion was made that we meant that this tax was to apply all across the board, to property and everything else. That is just nonsense. The United States, which I think can claim with some fairness


to be a little bit more capitalistic than this country, has a capital gains tax. It works and is effective. It applies specifically to dealings in the stock market; it has nothing to do with property.
To return to the planning aspect of what we need to do and where we need to go, may I say this. It seems to me the fact that the majority of people recognize that the central government has a responsibility for the economy today is full support for the idea of a coherent planning program. One of the other difficulties that loom in our way in Canada, and is a big bogey, is the whole question of provincial rights. We can certainly see that education has to be a fundamental part of any plan. It may be the whole key to our future, whether or not we are taking a socialistic interpretation. As long as we have one province holding the line, as Quebec indicates it is going to do, we are going to have difficulty in moving to national planning in order to attack the problems in education. If Quebec holds on to its point of view I think we may even reach the stage where we will find that the rest of the country will have to go ahead with national educational planning and let Quebec stay outside, as she has stayed outside in a number of other arrangements. If Quebec feel that it is so necessary for their own individuality and culture to remain outside in the educational field, then I think we will have to recognize that they have that right and, on the other hand, Quebec will have to recognize that the rest of Canada has a right to go ahead on a national basis with some sort of plan to pull us out of our educational problems.
That is an example of the kind of field I think we have to attack with planning. It is one of the fields to which I think we can point and say to this particular government, "You have not done what you indicated you would do". There is no use flaunting around the words of a man who is no longer here. Certainly as an educationist I and most of my colleagues, to my knowledge, had great respect for the late secretary of state for external affairs. We know that he proselytized across the country time after time, before he was a politician and when he was a politician, for a national approach to the higher education problem. He spelled it out in terms of junior colleges and the kind of support the government should give. That is the type of planning with which I thinir we should go ahead.
One of the points always made by antiplanners seems to be that it leads to a greater and greater build-up of the top-heavy civil service. Let us look at an example. I was checking the departments of this government

and their rate of growth; and, from what I can make out, the fastest growing department we have is the Department of Transport.
Yet that is a department in which almost every member of this house has a real interest. We are always calling on that department, and I think fairly, to extend its services.
If you stop and think of the scope of these services and what they mean, Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that a department of this kind must grow in order to fulfil its obligations. Consider for example its obligations in so far as television and radio communications are concerned, licence checks and that type of thing, or in the field of northern development, airports and airport development and the tie-in with our whole communications structure. That department is bound to get bigger and broader and be involved with faster and more complicated devices.
This matter of growth is something you just cannot shrug off. It is something that has to be thrown back at these people who are always calling for smaller and smaller government. In a field such as transportation I think we can and should call for what we have insisted on for some time, namely a national planning authority and some kind of regulatory authority. In the last few days we have had in a committee a long argument on freight rates. From the presentations that are being made it is obvious that this is more than a question of railways. It is a question that comes down to fundamental principles in our country, namely whether we should take the socialistic approach to our railways or whether we should try to put the clock back and go back to some kind of capitalistic approach. It is also evident that you cannot separate the railways from water transportation or truck transportation in any kind of regulatory control. If you give one regulation, it impedes it unfairly with respect to the others.
One of the obvious difficulties of the planning approach is that it is difficult. It is not easy. There is no simple formula, and experts can quite often be wrong. It is easy for people to look around the world and cite certain examples where the experts have been wrong. I think the favourite example is the labour government's groundnuts scheme in Africa just after the last war. We can get all kinds of examples of that kind. But really there is no choice but that of planning. There is no other choice. We cannot go back to any day that really never did exist in Canada, of complete dog eat dog, the market place ruling and the law of supply and demand. That situation just does not exist any more.
What our responsibility should be-and it is certainly a responsibility that this group tends to bear and that I hope our new party
The Budget-Mr. Morissette will tend to bear-is to do more detailed planning of where we should go. If that program does not appeal to the Canadian electorate and does not get their support, of course we shall be disappointed; but more than being disappointed, I think we shall rue the day.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) should be commended for his budget speech. His review of Canada's general economic position and his analysis of the public accounts for the year ending March 31 last, reveal on the one hand that his estimates of last year were accurate, which lends probability and validity to his estimates for the current year and, on the other hand, that legislation passed by this government has efficiently and decisively contributed to check the recession and launch our economy towards a new era of prosperity.
The facts brought out in the minister's speech also show that the gloomy forecasts of our Liberal and socialist friends were not to be taken seriously and were the result of an ill-contained spite rather than an objective and intelligent study of existing circumstances.
My colleagues will remember that the Minister of Finance had forecast, with regard to 1958, a gross national revenue of about 32 billion dollars. The facts have proved him right.
As a matter of fact the gross national revenue exceded that amount. According to the dominion bureau of statistics, it reached a figure of $32,184,000,000. Yet, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson), financial critic of the official opposition, has attempted to deride the minister's forecast. He has accused the Minister of Finance of picking that figure out of the air and of failing, in those estimates, to take into consideration the main components of the gross national revenue. The hon. member said, at that time, as can be seen on page 1465 of the official record of this house:
I suggest that the minister seems to have taken probably the most optimistic of all advice in calculating the gross national product. That leaves some doubt in the first instance, when we consider this matter of deficit, as to whether the revenue estimate of $4,660 million is attainable.
Everybody knows today that in 1958 the Minister of Finance was not over-optimistic, and that his forecast was a sound one, for the revenue which had been estimated at
2746	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Morissette $4,652 million actually amounted to $4,770 million. The facts, therefore, failed to justify the opposition's calculated pessimism.
Other members of the opposition had also made gloomy computations. Some of them had forecast the breakdown of our export trade. Others had indicated that the number of unemployed would reach a million. All of them were wrong, for our export trade has remained stable and the employment situation never deteriorated to the extent prophesied by our hon. friends. As the Minister of Finance stated the other day, the number of workers has gone up by 152,000 as compared to last year, and the number of unemployed itself is also lower than the year before.
On the whole, Mr. Speaker, and thanks especially to a fiscal policy and adequate legislation, the pattern of the Canadian economy has been sound in 1958. The recession was brought under control and under the impetus of a wise government policy the country's economy is showing signs of increased buoyancy.
It is both interesting and encouraging to note that the trend of the Canadian economy as a whole has been better than that of our neighbours. I should like here to make a brief comparative survey of this development on the basis of some of the most reliable tests of the economic situation. The figures I am going to use are found in the Labour Research, a review published by the Canadian Congress of Labour. According to this review, the seasonally adjusted gross national product in Canada reached $31,748 million in the third quarter of 1957. In the last quarter of 1957, it decreased to $31,460 million. In the first quarter of 1958 it had increased $31,684 million, and in the second quarter to $32,248 million. We are aware that this upward trend held out in the latter part of the year, and that the rate of increase was stepped up.
In the United States, at the end of 1957, the gross national product amounted to $438,900 million. In the first quarter of 1958, it was $425,800 million and, in the second quarter, $429 billion. Thus, it is easy to realize that the volume of gross national income in the United States was falling off, whereas Canada's gross national product had already begun to grow substantially. In other words, assuming that the gross national product figure reached in the third quarter of 1957 represents 100, we find that in the last quarter, it went down to 99.1 per cent, then up to 99.8 per cent in the first quarter of 1958 and as high as 101.6 in the second quarter of 1958. In the United States,


the situation is as follows: the figure in the third quarter of 1957 reached 100. The index decreased to 98.5 in the fourth quarter of 1957, to 95.6 in the first quarter of 1958, and stood at 96.3 in the second quarter of 1958.
In other words, while the downward trend in the volume of the gross national product occurred at the same time both in the United States and in Canada, it was never as marked in Canada as it was in the United States, and moreover, the gross national product had already started to increase in Canada while it was still declining in the United States.
Now, let us draw a parallel between available personal incomes. I mean the total volume of personal income, less direct taxes and especially income tax.
In Canada at the end of 1957, those incomes amounted to $21,480 million. In the first quarter of 1958, they went up 2.8 per cent, to reach $22,080 million; in the second quarter, they rose to $22,892 million. In the United States, the available personal incomes reached, in the third quarter of 1957, $308,700 million. In the fourth quarter, they dropped 0.6 per cent to $306,800 million. They again declined, in the first quarter of 1958, by 1.2 per cent to $305 billion. They went up again in the second quarter of 1958, when available personal incomes reached $307,500 million, which was still 0.4 per cent below the pre-recession level. There again, the Canadian economy is showing greater buoyancy.
It should be pointed out, Mr. Speaker, that the buoyancy, in Canada, of available personal income resulted in greater consumption, estimated at 3 per cent, between the third quarter of 1957 and the first quarter of 1958, while in the United States, it declined by nearly 1 per cent, as a result of a substantial decrease in the purchase of durable goods.
The greater strength of available personal income is due especially to the fact that old age pensions and other governmental transfer payments have been' increased, while there was a decrease in taxation rates.
There is now evidence that those government measures have had considerable effect on the expansion of our economy.
In Canada, the workers' income rose, in August 1957, to $1,305 million. I refer here to the over-all seasonally adjusted monthly income. After having gone down to $1,282

million at the end of 1957 that income rose to a new high of $1,316 million in May 1958, i.e. an increase of 0.8 per cent as compared to August 1957. In June, there was a slight decrease to $1,312 million, followed by a new rise to $1,317 million in July 1958, which exceeds the level reached in August 1957.
Let us now refer to the same statistics with regard to the United States. In August
1957,	workers' income reached $20,825 million. That figure kept declining until April
1958,	to reach the level of $20,075 million, i.e. a decrease of 3.6 per cent. They increased in May, June and July 1958. Worker incomes, both in Canada and in the United States, started to drop during the same period, and declined steadily until the end of 1957. However, while the decrease was felt until April 1958 in the United States, the trend was reversed in Canada in January 1958, and the index continued to rise steadily. In Canada, worker incomes did not drop as low as they did across the border, and they recovered earlier, at a more rapid pace and to a greater degree than in the United States.
Now if you compare industrial production Indexes in both countries, you again find that Canada's economy showed greater strength than that of the United States. Both production indexes began to drop at about the same time in early 1957, but while there was substantial recovery in Canada early in 1958, there was no marked recovery in the United States until mid 1958. Furthermore, the decline in industrial production was twice as great in the United States as in Canada. In July 1958, the industrial production index in Canada was 4.4 per cent below the point reached before the downswing, while in the United States, the gap was 8.2 per cent. In manufacturing, the situation was similar; in Canada, the index declined in 1957, but began to recover as early as January 1958. The rise continued into February, April, May and June. In July, the index reached a point 5.7 per cent below the level of February 1957. In the United States, the decline began in August 1957 and lasted until April 1958, when the trend was reversed. Thus, while manufacturing production declined earlier in Canada than in the United States, it dropped to a much lower level in the United States. Manufacturing production had been picking up for three months in Canada while it was still declining in the United States. In July 1958, in the United States, it stood at 6.8 cent below the peak registered before
The Budget-Mr. Morissette the decline; in Canada, it was only 5.7 per cent below the February 1957 level.
In Canada, the production index for durable goods, after reaching a peak in July 1956, began to drop until March 1958. At that time, the trend was reversed, and increases were registered in April, May, June and August 1958. In the latter month, the index stood at a point 12.7 per cent below the 1956 peak.
In the United States, the same index began to fall in December 1956. The downswing went on from September 1957 to April 1958. Having reached a low point of 20.6 per cent, the index then began to recover.
Here, in Canada, the production of durable goods weakened earlier than in the United States, but on the other hand, the decline was greater in the United States.
In Canada, the number of housing starts had reached a record of 145,400 units in the first quarter of 1955. Early in 1957, that number had decreased to 86,000, or 40.9 per cent.
From then on, though, a marked increase was recorded. In the first quarter of 1958, the number of starts reached a fantastic high of 175,600, 20.8 per cent above the pre-recession record. In the second quarter of 1958, they decreased to 162,500, still much higher than the pre-recession record.
In the United States, the highest number of starts, 1,435,000, had been reached in December 1954. In March 1957, they went down by 35 per cent and in February 1958, the decrease had reached 36.2 per cent.
In July, a recovery took place but it was still a long way from the high level reached before the economic slow-down.
The volume of home building has therefore declined less sharply in Canada and recovery has been infinitely stronger than in the United States. In Canada, home building permits for an amount of $86,712,000 had been issued in September 1955. In December 1956, this amount had dropped to $50,466,000, a decline of 41.8 per cent.
A new record was reached in November
1957.	The figure was then $92,539,000. This increase held out until February 1958, when the fantastic amount of $130,242,000 was reached. This was an increase of 50.2 per cent over the record pre-recession level. In June
1958,	the amount was still at the very high level of $101,133,000, or 16.6 per cent above the pre-recession record.
In the United States, a record was reached in November 1956, when the total amount
2748	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Morissette was $1,468,000,000. A year later, in November 1957, there was a very slight improvement. From then on, there was a drop until May 1958 followed by an increase in August 1958.
The lowest level was 9.1 per cent lower than that of November 1956 and 9.4 per cent lower than that of November 1957. The August 1958 high was 2.6 per cent over that of November 1956 and 2.3 per cent higher than in November 1957. While recession started earlier and was sharper in Canada than in the United States, the recovery was much stronger in Canada. The whole credit for this should go to the government, for making the necessary funds available to house builders. We know that 50 per cent of the housing starts in 1958 in Canada were financed through the National Housing Act.
In the field of industrial construction, it should be noted that while the decrease in Canada was sharper than in the United States, recovery was noticeable by May 1958, while the decline was continuing in the United States.
In business construction, the American economy was somewhat better than our own.
Let us now compare statistics relating to corporation profits. I refer here to profits before taxes. An unprecedented high had been reached in that field during the first and third quarters of 1956. From the third quarter of 1956, they registered a decline lasting up to the first quarter of 1958. From the second quarter of 1958, corporation profits were on their way up.
The United States have experienced a somewhat similar movement, but the decline was twice as sharp there as in Canada.
Let us look now at the trends of employment in some sectors of the economy. In Canada, the employment index in manufactures reached a high in December 1956. From then on, it decreased until April 1958, but in May, June, July and August 1958, it showed an increase. In the United States, the pre-recession high was reached in December 1956.
From then on there has been a decline until May 1958. During the following months, conditions showed some improvement. The decline began at the same time in the United States and in Canada. It has been checked earlier in Canada, and it never reached the same proportions as in the United States. From that point of view, Canada stood up
IMr. Morissette.]

better than our neighbour. The same holds true for the employment index in the production of durable goods. The peak was reached in Canada in November 1956 and was followed by an irregular downward trend until April 1958. In May and June, there was an increase.
In the United States, the highest level was reached in December 1956, followed by a decline until May 1958. The development of the unemployment index in that sector of the economy is very much similar in both countries though, here again, we find that recovery is firmer in Canada. The employment index with regard to the production of non-durable goods reached its peak in Canada in August 1957. A downward trend was noted until March 1958, but from then on there was an increase. In the United States, the peak was reached in November 1955, and was followed by a decline until March 1958. From then on, an increase was noted, but, here again, it must be said that the downward trend in the United States was twice as marked as in Canada.
We may therefore conclude that, after all, Canadian economy has stood up well in a period which was extremely difficult for North America. Recession is one of those things the Conservatives inherited from the Liberals. The facts I have shown prove that the recession has hit bottom and that recovery is now well on its way.
In his annual report the governor of the Bank of Canada stressed that "in the last quarter of 1958, the gross national product was higher by 4 per cent in Canada and 2 per cent in the United States, than the previous record figure."
The policy of relaxation with regard to monetary conditions which the government applied at the end of 1957 contributed more than any other factor to check the recession and to promote economic recovery. As a matter of fact, the recession has not been as severe or as protracted as certain people had foreseen. This is an a posteriori confirmation of the government's wise policy.
The Canadian public is grateful to the government and to the Minister of Finance who, in a difficult period, have practised a bold policy which, in the first place, checked the progress of the recession, then stopped it completely and, finally, brought about a strong economic recovery.

speechtext:
I believe I heard the voice of the member for Roberval (Mr. Tremblay). I also note that the member for Joliette-L'As-somption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) has already started to interject. If he really wants to coo, he might wait till I am through with my remarks.
Mr. Speaker, the budget brought down on April 9 last by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) came as no surprise, as far as the deficit is concerned, and despite the government's efforts to have the people accept this general tax increase, I think the people are fully aware that this government's election promises were nothing but a smoke screen and had no other purpose than to win votes.
We also recall that the pre-election concessions granted by this government in the taxation field included reductions involving about $178 million.
It follows that such generosity is more than cancelled by the $245 million to be taken from the taxpayers by the end of this year, and by the $352 million which the new taxes will cost us in a full year.
There is no denying that the tax increase will mostly hurt the consumer, because most of the business firms that are being taxed will include the taxes in their sale price. Consumer purchasing power, which already was extremely low, will be further lowered by the government's action.
The consumer purchasing power being reduced, that will substantially affect the demand and, in my opinion, the supply will certainly be affected as well. It should not be surprising if, as a result of that decline in the purchasing power, some concerns were obliged to cut down their production, which would certainly not help solve the unemployment problem nor bring the revenue which the Minister of Finance seems to be so much in need of.
The Budget-Mr. Racine
The Minister of Finance has admitted a deficit of $616 million for the fiscal year 1958-1959.
That deficit would certainly have been more palatable if it had contributed, in some way, to an economic recovery or had helped at least to partially reduce unemployment, if not completely.
That deficit is not either the immediate result of an increase in social benefits, such as family allowances, for instance, which would have helped increase the purchasing power of the taxpayers as well as stimulate business and industry.
The position of the federal treasury and the financial problems facing the minister are evidence, as well as the very picture, of the difficulties which workers, farmers and industrialists in this country must face.
Such financial unbalance is the very picture of the sad economic situation prevailing in several fields in Canada, and which is causing unceasing concern to a great number of our fellow-citizens, especially if we consider the nearly total absence of governmental measures designed to help remedy such a situation.
We realize also that the financial situation of the government has deteriorated during the two years of Conservative administration. For instance, the funded debt, according to table 2a, page 2412 of Hansard, has gone up from $15.4 billion in 1956 to $15.6 billion in 1959. For the same period, the total debt rose from $19.1 billion to $20.2 billion, and the percentage of the gross national product, which was 41.7 in 1956, has gone down to 36.3.
In spite of increased taxation, the present Minister of Finance will be able to boast of a rather unenviable record: that of having increased the national debt by more than $1 billion in two years.' His forecasts for 19591960 are hardly more encouraging, since he expects another deficit of $393 million.
Are we going to have, under the present government, a continuous and yearly increase in taxation? The Minister of Finance stated on television, the night he introduced his budget, that he could not say when he would be able to introduce a balanced budget.
And yet, Mr. Speaker, when he was in the opposition, the same minister was asking for a balanced budget, and was not criticizing Conservative deficits, but rather Liberal surpluses, which contributed to reduce the national debt.

The Budget-Mr. Racine
The Minister of Finance is far from improving our financial position. He faces the same problem as last year, and has admitted himself that in spite of the deficit he expects, he will again be facing the same problems next year.
If, at that time, he uses the same methods, the consumer will be paying again, and we will again witness a further drop in our purchasing power.
Just to show the inconsistency of the present administration, let us take an item which has been increased, as evidence that election promises are not being carried out.
Here is a statement made by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on February 17, 1958 at Brantford, as reported in the Toronto Daily Star of February 18:
(Text):
Prime Minister Diefenbaker last night dropped a clear hint that the taxes on cigarettes, cigars and tobacco soon may be cut.
He told an audience of 1,400 that no industry in Canada suffers a greater degree of taxation than the tobacco industry.
Tobacco growers, he said, are the one segment of agriculture that has not received the attention it deserves, although growers long have clamoured for government aid.
The Prime Minister added: "We want to give them this assistance. We are having a study made of this industry to see what action is needed to give tobacco growers a reasonable return and some security for their efforts."
The tax on a 33 cent pack of cigarettes now is about 18 cents, made up of an excise tax, and excise duty, and a 10 per cent sales tax.
The study probably will be made by the Department of Finance and any ensuing tax cut could be introduced in time for the 1958-59 federal budget expected in May.
To the Brantford audience, living on the northern fringe of Ontario's tobacco belt-where production has jumped from 63,000 acres in 1943 to 120,000 in 1956-the Prime Minister's hint appeared an effective vote catcher.
(Translation):
I wonder if, after presenting this budget, the Prime Minister could go back to Brantford, repeat those statements and make as many friends among the voters.
This budget also fails to justify any hope of higher benefits under existing social legislation or of any further welfare measures.
May I quote what the Prime Minister said in Hull on February 25, 1958, as reported in the Montreal Star of February 26, 1958:
(Text):
The Prime Minister told his Hull audience of some 850 persons that some features of the United States plan would have to be altered before it could be fitted on top of the present Canadian program of $55 monthly pensions paid to all at 70.


He detailed the payments which he said are made under the United States plan to those on average incomes:	between $88.50 and $98.50 a
month for single workers retiring at age 65; $132.80 a month for a husband and wife retiring at age 65; death benefits of $255; disability payments starting at age 50.
(Translation):
More unkept promises! Mr. Speaker, if I wanted to list these in detail in this house, it would take me much longer than my allotted forty minutes.
However, if we examine all the Prime Minister's election promises, we find with some surprise that he has not indicated his position with regard to family allowances which are, to my mind, the most significant social legislation we have in Canada.
Last year, on the same occasion, that is during the budget debate, I spoke at length about family allowances and showed that at that time the cost of living index regarding family needs had doubled since they were introduced in 1944 and paid out in 1945, and that it was the government's responsibility to increase them adequately.
No one need be an economist to realize that the family allowances set up in 1945 no longer have the same buying power in 1959, and I believe it is the government's duty to correct that situation so as to provide for the needs and requirements of Canadian homes.
If the Prime Minister made no reference to this matter during the last elections, are we to understand that family allowances are of no interest to him or that he wittingly or unwittingly overlooked them? Under the circumstances, I cannot account for the Prime Minister's position on this matter. On the other hand, there were hon. members who did not hesitate to tackle the subject, during the election campaign and to come out with their promises so that I wonder why they kept mum about it last year. was happy to get farther and farther away from the opposition.

members opposite will be doing the same.

That is why if the Quebec government cares to offer a suggestion, to make an official proposal, an appropriate and constructive one, I am positive that this government will consider it with great care and that, eventually, a proper solution will be found in this field.
I am in full agreement with my hon. friend from Sherbrooke. I am sure that, if the Quebec government really wanted to make a constructive proposal, the present government would consider it with great interest, as the previous government would have done too. But, if we accept my hon. friend's statement we have to infer that in the last 7 years since those grants were offered, the province of Quebec or rather the Union Nationale government or even the premier himself, (Mr. Duplessis), have failed to come out with some constructive suggestion, some official or appropriate proposal in order to settle that problem.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I add my congratulations to those already expressed to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) for his excellent presentation of the budget. May I also extend my congratulations to the hon. members who have preceded me in this budget debate for the contributions which they have made through their budget speeches.
In the presentation of the budget the minister has given the Canadian people a frank and honest appraisal of Canada's economic position, and a clear-cut explanation which Canadians have learned to expect from our capable and realistic Minister of Finance. Editorial comment regarding the budget has been interesting, and for the most part the opinions expressed showed satisfaction. There has been a general agreement that the minister's budget is one well suited to our present economic position. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, I speak for all Canadians when I say I am pleased to see indications which definitely point to recovery. The fact that there is less unemployment than a year ago and there are more Canadians employed in Canada than one year ago is extremely encouraging and proof of the wisdom of Conservative government policies.
The provision of money by this parliament in its first session made possible more than 163,000 housing starts in Canada in 1958. That is truly an amazing record and one which surpasses the previous record year of 1955 by about 25,000. The availability of this money for housing was a notable factor in creating employment in my own riding. In the riding of Kingston in 1951 the value of housing for which building permits were issued totalled slightly less than $1 minion; in 1957 this figure stood at slightly over $2 million; in 1958 in the city of Kingston this figure jumped to $4,725,000. That is concrete evidence of the value of the government's policy to provide money for the construction of homes.
Both labour and contractors in my riding have been doing an excellent job carrying on winter construction. However, I think that

The Budget-Mr. Allmark we Canadians have a great deal to learn about winter construction. Nevertheless it is apparent that never before has construction been carried on to the extent it has been carried on this winter. I think it is most important that we intensify the educational program which has already had excellent results but which if carried on in a thorough and extensive manner will result in a further expansion of construction during the winter months.
It has been quite remarkable to watch the construction of buildings at Queen's University during the past winter. There has been excellent co-operation by the university. As a result, our Kingston tradesmen and labourers have benefited through this season when normally employment would be at a low level. I think our own government departments which are responsible for construction should make it their policy to award contracts at a time of the year when it would permit the building to be at such a stage that construction could be carried on during the winter months under the most favourable conditions. It is useless for the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) to publicize the necessity for providing winter work unless, of course, our own government departments co-operate and set an example to the general public.
Mr. Speaker, since this is the first occasion on which I have spoken on a budget or throne speech to date, I trust that you will grant me the privilege of making some reference to the riding which I represent. I refer to the historical riding of Kingston, an area comprising the fast growing city of Kingston, the townships of Kingston, Storring-ton and Pittsburgh and the islands of Wolfe, Howe and Simcoe. I do not intend to trace the events in the long and historical existence of my riding, but I think I should mention the fact that the people I represent have displayed an exceptional quality of judgment down through the years. My electorate chose John A. Macdonald, then 29 years of age, as Kingston's member to the government of Canada, on October 15, 1844. This quality of good judgment has obviously remained with the people. This fact was proven last autumn when the Speaker of the House of Commons was chosen as the recipient of an honorary doctor's degree at the fall convocation at Queen's University. It was my privilege to attend this convocation; and may I say that I was extremely proud to witness our able Speaker being honoured by the university in my riding.
We who are the residents of this riding are proud of the part we have played in Canadian history but may I stress the fact that in these days of growth and expansion in Canada we are not living in the past. We

are not afraid-as are some on the other side of the house-that Canada is facing ruin. We believe we will share in the great and rapid expansion which will take place in Canada in the years ahead. We believe that Kingston will share in the prosperity which will result from the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway which will carry the ships of all nations half-way across this vast continent.
It is to be regretted, Mr. Speaker-and I have said this before in the house-that those responsible for the planning of the seaway did not have the foresight or the good judgment to use the Canadian channel in the western 25 miles of the St. Lawrence river. I think that the hon. members of the house should be aware of the fact that before the building of the seaway there were approximately 30 miles of the Kingston to Montreal section of the St. Lawrence in United States waters. The decision to put the Snell and Eisenhower locks on the United States side placed 20 miles in United States waters, and the decision to use the United States channel rather than the Canadian channel in the Kingston area-and this channel had been the shipping channel since shipping in the St. Lawrence began-placed another 25 miles in United States waters, so that now approximately 75 miles of this 168-mile stretch of river is completely on the United States side of the boundary.
Kingston is a thriving port, handling one million to one and one-half million tons of seaway cargo a year, I think it is interesting to note that with the proposed seaway tolls this represents $600,000 to $700,000 yearly. That is a substantial contribution toward the $28 million required annually to amortize the seaway over a 50-year period. It is difficult to understand why such a port was ignored by the Liberal government when for a small expenditure the channel could have been retained in Canadian waters.
On June 28 of this year the people of the Kingston area will welcome Her Majesty's yacht Britannia which will carry the Queen of Canada and His Royal Highness Prince Philip to the city of Kingston which was once the capital of Canada. We are distressed to realize that the Britannia will not follow that same Canadian channel taken by Baron Sydenham, governor of Canada, when he arrived in Kingston on May 28, 1841 to open the parliament of Canada. I hope that on this trip which the Queen makes across Canada there will be a minimum of ceremony and an opportunity for the royal couple to enjoy the scenic beauty and the many places of historic interest in our country. By our actions this year let us convince our Queen that she may enjoy in

Canada that leisure and rest which will make this trip an enjoyable vacation.
This junction of the St. Lawrence river and the lakes is also the terminal for both river and lake pilots. There appears to be the opinion that the crews of foreign-going ships are capable of piloting their ships through the restricted waters of our inland system. There is no one who will deny that foreign ships' officers are capable navigators, but this is a skill of little importance in lake and river shipping. It has been said that the safety of the seaway is paramount, and this also applies to our marine installations throughout the lakes, to our ships and to the lives of Canadian sailors. If we in Canada are to be assured of the degree of safety necessary then we must rely on the experience and ability of those men who have spent their lives learning the skill of ship handling and learning the hundreds of miles of river and restricted channels in our inland waters.
We have in my riding four of Canada's nine penitentiaries, one of these being the women's penitentiary. Kingston is also the location of a staff college for the training of penitentiary officers. I do not suggest that those of us who live near the penal institutions are therefore experts in the matter of penal reform; and I trust that the observations I am about to make will not be construed by the members of this house as being those of an authority. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) has within his department a correctional planning board which is at present studying the penal system in Canada. To this group may I suggest that the majority of female inmates come from the same fair province as does the minister. It is my observation that his province would be a much more suitable location for this institution. I suggest that this handsome limestone building now being used as a women's prison might well be converted into a modern inmates' hospital. The excellent Queen's University medical school is undoubtedly responsible for providing in Kingston hospital facilities comparable to the best on the continent. A new modern penitentiary hospital could enjoy the benefits which this medical school would provide.
May I also request the Minister of Justice to consider Kingston as the site for a new minimum security institution. There are many advantages in having prisons grouped in one area. Kingston, located as it is halfway between Toronto and Montreal, is ideally situated since it makes the visiting by the inmates' relatives easier and this visiting privilege, I understand, is an important factor in the rehabilitation of the inmate. If the
The Budget-Mr. Allmark Kingston area is fortunate in obtaining a new institution I would suggest that it be located a few miles to the north of the city rather than to the east or west, where in a few years it would be encircled by residential development.
The people of my riding have a fair knowledge of penal institutions. The officers for the most part are residents of our city and we appreciate the problems which exist in the operation of penitentiaries, and we are indeed pleased to have them located in our area. There is one point which is very apparent, and that is that the present Minister of Justice has had dumped in his lap a penal system totally inadequate to take care of the needs of a country of 17 million people. This is a direct result of the failure of the Liberal government to take those steps which are necessary to increase the accommodation in these institutions.
One of the scenic beauty spots of our country is that point of land at the junction of the great Cataraqui river and the St. Lawrence, where the royal military college is situated. Many of the members of this house had the opportunity to visit R.M.C. on army day last year, and I am convinced that they were impressed with the natural beauty of this location. On the very tip of this point of land is located Fort Frederick, a very beautiful and historic old fort which in recent years has been allowed, unfortunately, to fall into a bad state of disrepair. I would like at this time to express my appreciation of the very able and expert assistance of the Kingston historical society, which assisted me in bringing to the attention of the minister the condition of Fort Frederick. This fort is being repaired and will further enhance the appearance of these beautiful grounds. The decision of the Conservative government to do this work is to be commended.
I would like to remind the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) that the removal of those houses with which I am sure he is acquainted located at the north of the playing field at R.M.C. would make possible the conversion of this particular area into a beauty spot in keeping with the remainder of the college grounds. There are thousands of United States tourists each year who view our Kingston military installations and the college as they pass along No. 2 highway. It is my opinion it is extremely important to Canada that these buildings and grounds be kept in a condition of which we, as Canadians, may be proud.
I am very pleased that the route of the Britannia will carry Her Majesty through the thousand islands on her holiday this summer. This is a magnificent sight and one which
2756	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Allmark should thrill our royal visitors. One of our great assets in the thousand islands are our national parks. Pleasure boats varying in size from the small outboard motorboats to the large palatial yachts pack the dock facilities provided by the Canadian government. Here too there has been an unfortunate lack of foresight in the national park area, with the result that today there are far too few docks to accommodate the vast number of boats in this area. Obviously we would not wish to prevent our United States visitors from using these national parks, so there appears only one solution. If Canadian boat owners are to enjoy their own Canadian islands we must build additional dock facilities. I can assure the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) that the provision of additional docks in the parks of the thousand islands will make him a very popular person among the great number of boat owners.
Mr. Speaker, we have in my riding a very large and growing tourist industry. Not only in the city, but in the country to the north there are hundreds of beautiful lakes, and it is truly a fisherman's paradise. There is presently set up an international Kingston-Cape Vincent bridge committee which comprises six United States and six Canadian members. Its purpose is to promote the construction of an international bridge in this area to facilitate the crossing of the St. Lawrence and thereby further increasing the tourist business to this lakeland area. If this bridge is built it will be indeed a tremendous asset. I would like to point out the spirit of goodwill and co-operation which exists between the Canadian cities and towns in this area and those across the border in the United States. This is indicated by the ability of these neighbours to join together for the promotion of a project beneficial to both countries. May I commend here the members of this committee for their sincere effort and enthusiasm in this project.
I earlier made some modest reference to Kingston's place in history and to the fact that in 1844 Kingston was represented in the parliament of upper and lower Canada by John A. Macdonald. May I close, Mr. Speaker, by saying that Kingston riding has been denied for some years the privilege of having the name of Sir John A. Macdonald placed on the pages of Hansard by a Kingston member of the same political faith as the old chieftain. I do so today with humility and respect for that great statesman, whose leadership, wisdom and vision foresaw in this united dominion the land of opportunity we have today.

Mr. Speaker, I want to express myself in French in order to deal with a few matters for the benefit of my fellow citizens, i.e. hon. members from the province of Quebec. I believe it appropriate to speak on behalf of my fellow-citizens in northern Ontario with regard to the serious problems of higher education in this country, of federal-provincial relations and, lastly, of grants to universities.
I rise as the representative of a riding which has the youngest bilingual university in this country, i.e. the University of Sudbury, which, for several years, has had the opportunity of benefiting from federal grants put at the disposal of Canadian universities.
As an hon. member explained just now, I realize how easy it is to make political speeches about that problem and to repeat the words "autonomy" and "constitutional", but I think that the 50 hon. members or so from the province of Quebec who are sitting on the government benches would be well advised to take steps to come to some agreement with the federal government and the government of Quebec so that students from that province might enjoy the benefits of higher education which federal grants could provide and therefore be on the same footing as their fellow students elsewhere in this country.
I have no intention to refer to discussions regarding the constitutional point of view, but it seems reasonable to assume that the fathers of confederation, when wording the British North America Act, possibly did not imagine what higher technical education would cost in 1959.
In order to prove that allegation, I would like to quote remarks from professor Lower's volume From Colony to Nation. On page 343 of that book, professor Lower deals with the question of higher education in Canada in 1867 and he says:

In higher education all the larger colleges and universities of eastern Canada had been founded with the exception of Western Ontario and McMaster. Some of these institutions, such as Queen's, already had several faculties. Both Queen's and Victoria had faculties of medicine and there was also a medical school in Toronto. Queen's had 18 professors and 180 students, Victoria had 200 students, Trinity seven professors, University College, Toronto, nine. Every institution in the

country, with the exception of Toronto and Dal-housie, was denominational and there was about them all as there was about every school, too, a strong religious flavour.

Students bodies were larger, but not much larger than they had been thirty years before: Universities were for the education of persons who took education seriously and expected to go into a profession; the great modern movement of mass 'education' had not begun.

I should like to say a few words, Mr. Speaker, on the matter of municipal and federal relations. This is of the greatest importance in my riding because it contains rather small and young municipalities located in rocky areas where construction of public services is most costly. When I spoke for the first time in the house last year I suggested that the government should think of the burden of taxation on the people living in mining areas brought about by the high cost of services in the municipalities. I suggested that the government should find a solution for the problem of double taxation whereby the ratepayer pays for all local services and also pays a second tax to the treasury in Ottawa on the money so spent.
Before the election the municipalities were promised a meeting with the federal government, a meeting at which they would find solutions to their local problems through federal channels. Later came the conversion loan which, as is known by all municipal officers, hurt their position very much by raising the rate of interest and creating many difficulties in the sale of their debentures. Taxation is high in the mining municipalities. The people employed in the mines must live nearby and they live in a rocky region where it is definitely more costly to build homes. I believe that the government should assist Canadians to realize their ambition to own their own homes. A system whereby money spent for municipal taxes would at least to some extent be exempt from federal taxation would be one way of equalizing the burden of home ownership in Canada. It is obvious to all that it is more costly in certain areas to have the services which Canadians are entitled to have under our standard of living and this type of tax exemption would certainly be beneficial.
