Mr. Speaker, these tables will bring into vivid focus the fact that the port of Vancouver, unknown largely throughout Canada, handles a foreign tonnage in excess of that of Bristol in the United Kingdom, Capetown in South Africa and the Clyde navigation trust in the United Kingdom. I feel that it is right that hon. members of this house should be advised of these rather important facts. I would also further state that only fractional, under the total foreign tonnages is the total of Vancouver compared with that of the great world ports of Sydney, Australia, Calcutta and the port of Montreal.
I would further state that in this connection I wish to draw direct reference to certain specific suggestions. I would point to the arrivals in the year 1957. The total for the national harbours board was 49,421. The ships and vessels arriving at the port of Vancouver totalled 31,433, or 60 per cent of those arriving in our national harbours board ports in Canada. I would further like to point out that of the total of national harbours board recorded departures of vessels, namely 49,031 ships, 30,997 sailed from the port of Vancouver or over 60 per cent of the total in this dominion. The registered tonnages arriving and departing from the port represent 40 per cent of the total registered tonnages in this dominion. As to cargo, 29 per cent of all the cargo tonnages in and out of national harbours board ports passed or under the first Lions Gate bridge at the First Narrows in the port of Vancouver.
Set against this record and in tragic reference to the administrations of the past, in many instances the administration of the national harbours board was not left at the discretion of the board but was handled through the discretionary powers of the former minister of transport who unfortunately is not with us at this time. Despite this, in 1957, following the pattern through the years of Liberal administration, 6 per cent of the total amount spent by the national harbours board on maintenance of ports was spent on the port of Vancouver. I would point out that this 6 per cent represents no charges for ice-breaking. It represents no capital cost relative to the construction of seaways. In saying that, Mr. Speaker, I wish to stress that the people of British Columbia do not in any way criticize any capital development anywhere in Canada. We endorse it; we wish it well. We just ask that in the future-and indeed I am sure that this will be the case-the tragic pattern which has led to the distressing conditions in this great port of the world will not continue as it did under the former administration.

I should also like to draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that on capital account spending, following a pattern established again under the former administration and followed for many years, 5 per cent of the total spending for capital development went into the port of Vancouver in 1957. That pattern was a tragic one that can be traced throughout our history during the years of Liberal administration. Again we say in respect of the administration and the difficulties experienced in this great port, that it was indeed Canada's Cinderella port. As far as the former minister of transport was concerned, it was hidden 3,000 miles from Ottawa and across the Rocky mountains. That was the measure of concern that was given to this industrial and commercial facility which provides Canada with berthing for 60 per cent of all the vessels arriving at and departing from national harbours board administered ports in this nation.
I have already stated that the port of Vancouver makes no call on the government to provide ice-breaking facilities. In addition, along with the ports on the east and west coasts, it provides berthing and harbour facilities for vessels 12 months of the year, providing stability to commerce throughout the full 12-month period and does not curtail the movement or in any way impede the matters of trade and commerce at any period of the year.
Basically in the port of Vancouver our largest movements are of grain, livestock, coal, chemicals and oil, in addition to British Columbia's own world outstanding export of lumber, finished and in logs.
We have over the past years, as indicated by the figures and the comparisons I have given, suffered acute congestion in the harbour, which I point out definitely most directly affects the ability of that port to service the needs of Canada's industries. The speed with which a ship may arrive in port, discharge its cargo and again depart with a load aboard, the turnaround, indicates the basic cost factor with which that port is able to handle its input of tonnages. If a port becomes stagnant by virtue of delays then there is an increased cost factor involved, it ceases to serve the needs of this exporting nation; and it matters not how well your other freight carriers may discharge their responsibilities and carry their loads, you cannot meet the needs of commerce.
I would point out in considering the Vancouver situation that in 1957 from a maintenance cost $207,860 was spent in the port of Vancouver, $8,000 less than was spent in the port of Churchill, to handle 132 inbound and outbound vessels as compared with the figure given earlier of 31,433. I think these figures

point out the tragic need and necessity which faced the Minister of Transport on taking office and reviewing the general conditions and situation surrounding this great natural facility. And what was found? I would like some of the former administration to listen to this.
Here is a port surrounded by mountains, limited in its foreshore development upon the recovery of gravel from the floor of the harbour to construct headlands. And what have they done? For years the favoured few garnered permits for the recovery and removal of gravel for 10 cents a cubic yard to sell to the commercial market at fantastic profits. And this, tragically enough, they did.
Perhaps that accounts for the quotation I would like to read from Bruce Hutchison's "The Fraser", which I would point out was printed and published in 1950. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that you and hon. members do not recognize Bruce Hutchison as an outstanding Tory propagandist. On page 197 of "The Fraser", for all to read, is this tragic statement:
In the shelter of this mushroom aristocracy, and usually with the aid of its campaign funds, Vancouver has produced some of the worst politics in Canada. The famous machine that has dominated public life almost without interruption for more than thirty years, has appointed its princelings to Senate and bench, has won elections with more money than prayers and always found that investment profitable, is about as efficient and ruthless as any in the nation. Governments, in both Victoria and Ottawa, have often tried to shake it but they have never succeeded, for it can deliver the votes.
But in 1957, and again last March, that machine could not deliver the votes, and it has been one of the jobs of the Minister of Transport to bring into focus and bring into function a proper policy so that in future these valuable assets of fill which can be recovered from the harbour bed and laid on the foreshore to guarantee that the development of this great harbours future could go forward. That policy, as I said last spring to my constituents, the minister has endorsed.
At this time I wish to give notice to the Minister of Transport, who unfortunately is not here, that some commitments had been made prior to the institution of this policy and certain permits are still running which will terminate this spring. I believe one has been renewed for a period of two years. I do not wish to be unreasonable, nor do I think my constituents would wish me to be unreasonable, but I will assure you that I will be a watch dog to see that when it terminates in two years no more raids on this great asset shall be undertaken.
The port of Vancouver, definitely reflecting this unimaginative program with the years of withholding the necessary funds for proper maintenance of the harbour has brought
The Budget-Mr. Payne into focus today the urgent need for certain development and planning. Proper utilization in the future is a responsibility which we owe the generations which are yet unborn and the future needs of the harbour and the tonnages that the port will have to discharge. I feel that we should embark upon a very broad study to assure its proper utilization and development, and if necessary search the world for the outstanding engineers and consultants necessary to lay forth these plans. These, I would point out again, should be given authority, and the harbour authority should be extended so that proper negotiations can be conducted between the city of Vancouver, the city of North Vancouver and the other four municipalities which surround Burrard inlet. Because without this it is impossible to bring into being plans for imaginative development programs, which our port needs if it is to survive and service this nation's and the west coast's needs. This authority must also call upon the department of Indian affairs, which I should mention holds very valuable strategic properties lying along the foreshore. It is important not only to Vancouver and the commercial needs of western Canada; it is also a requirement as far as the Indians are concerned. It will give them an agency through which these lands could be recovered, put to the best possible use, bringing to them as a result the highest potential returns.
Very urgently needed today, particularly on the main waterfront of Vancouver itself, is a high level approach road. Through topsyturvy development in the past, no proper road access exists in many areas, be it for the movement of freight or be it for fire protection on the waterfront. This capital spending would amount to millions, but if our port is not going to be strangled it must be included in future plans and at an early date.
I would like through you, Mr. Speaker, to advise this house that the Vancouver Wharves Limited have during these past ten days or two weeks announced the construction, on the north shore of Burrard inlet a new facility which will provide the basic deepsea wharfage need which I mentioned in the throne speech debate at the last session was so urgently required. This will provide the newly developed Pacific Great Eastern railway with the outlet to the ocean so badly needed. We are pleased to see this program going forward, and I trust that the minister and the national harbours board will see that no impediments are placed in the way of this development so that this essential program may proceed. Also, since last speaking to the house, Pacific Coast Bulk Terminals Limited have developed on the south shore a bulk loading facility so that in future,
27G6

The Budget-Mr. Payne I believe as of June this year, bulk tonnages and cargoes of coal, sulphur, chemicals and products of mines can be shipped from the port of Vancouver and will no longer require movement across the border and shipment from the port of Seattle.
One difficulty which today has caused more concern than any other-and this certainly was not only engendered but fostered by the former administration-has to do with the terminal railway facilities around the harbour. I must point out that at this time this great port which is today moving tonnages 15 times in excess of those handled by the port of Portland, Oregon, has no central terminal rail facilities. Instead, we have a complex and confused arrangement of railway switching charges under which, for instance, a C.N.R. box car delivered to a C.F.R. port for trackage outlet may be delayed for eight days and, in the process, have to pay exorbitant charges based on tonnage. Linking the north shore with the south shore we have the Second Narrows bridge; the old bridge, not the new highway traffic bridge which was the subject of tragic attention in this house last year. The old Second Narrows bridge was also the focus of attention in this house when a private bill was discussed. At that time I endeavoured to point out how essential a part the old Second Narrows bridge would play in a proper harbour authority terminal rail facility. Today I should like to call on the Minister of Transport to give serious and urgent consideration to bringing into being an adequate harbours board terminal railway facility based on the pattern existing in the port of Montreal so that this ridiculous and artificial obstruction to the movement of our trade and commerce may end forever.
These are but a few of the problems which face the harbour. We have seen over the years, in every city in all nations where harbours develop, that bridges become an essential part of the necessary facilities. I must confess that it is with special satisfaction that I find that bridges owned and operated by the national harbours board, or bridges which are being built and which are to be owned or operated by the board, exist today. I will name two-the Jacques Cartier bridge, with a capital cost of over $20,080,000, to be operated under a toll authority by the national harbours board, and the Champlain bridge with approximately $32 million of capital cost. I trust that this may be considered a new policy on the part of the government, for I am sure that the people of Halifax will join with those of us on the lower mainland of British Columbia in urging the need for assistance in particular areas where bridges are required over navigable

waters and in making the plea that the national harbours board or some other national body or administrative entity should be able to assist in relieving communities of the inordinately high cost which they must inevitably face in building bridges high enough to span navigable waters and at the same time, provide for the free movement of ships.
There is another situation which I think calls for immediate attention and inclusion in planning if the outlet to the world of commerce of which I have been speaking is to operate with any degree of efficiency. And in saying this I should like to point out that over 60 per cent of the world's population live today within 183 miles of the Pacific shore coast.
This final suggestion has to do with the port of Squamish, served, as it is, by the Pacific Great Eastern railroad from the north. This port is capable of providing good possibilities for the development of useful additional deep sea wharfage facilities in an area with which the port of Vancouver is closely connected and I submit that it would be tragic for this new port and tragic for the future both of the port of Squamish and of the port of Vancouver if any development undertaken were not to go forward on a complementary basis. I suggest that this port should be included as a satellite, or as an integral part of the administration of the port of Vancouver itself.
With these remarks I now leave the subject of the harbour for a moment, though not entirely because I wish to refer again to my initial statement and that is to the great and profound faith I put in the theory of administration by the national harbours board. I must state, however, that the activities which have already gone on and the developments which have taken place, the facts and figures of the past and the activities within the port of Vancouver, bring into focus one thing which I think the house today should consider carefully. This is the fact that management authorities within each port and unit are on a highly powerful and personal level. It must of necessity be that way. I think we should take a second look at the personnel who are engaged in administrative areas such as this, especially at those who have in the past, as the record proves, so completely failed to justify the faith placed in them in the discharge of their responsibilities to this nation. How in the world can we have faith in their ability, judgment and vision with regard the future planning which must go forward in order to provide for the facilities and needs of the future?
Mr. Speaker, I thank you again for this opportunity to present to the house a case which is as vital as this one is to the people

of the lower mainland. I trust we may see no continuance in the future of the tragic policies of the past. I am sure we shall not see this with respect to the port of Vancouver.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In rising to take part in this debate, I extend appreciation to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) for the work he must have put into the preparation of the budget. I judge that the time and effort which must go into the preparation of this most formidable document, irrespective of how the budget may be received, is considerable, and I think the minister and his officials should be shown appreciation for their discharge of this task. Another step has been taken along the fiscal road of the nation's business by the presentation of this year's budget. It is now part of the permanent history of Canada. It will, very likely, be the basis of discussion on many future occasions, if only for the purpose of comparison in election campaigns yet to come. Time will tell. It is now the subject to the forefront at this present time.
This debate is following the pattern of other budget debates. Party spokesmen add up the items, make calculations and come up with totals that are widely different. Some leave out relevant items and others include them which leads me to believe that an old saying is no longer true. That saying is, "Liars can figure, but figures do not lie." The arguments pro and con presented thus far in this debate, like those presented in other budget debates, suggest on the one hand that the government has presented a splendid budget, while on the other hand suggest that this budget will be detrimental to the country.
The government spokesmen contend that we are in a period of economic recovery, that there is a marked improvement in the trend of employment and earnings; an improvement in the volume of retail sales; that corporate profits have increased; and that there is no present evidence of overinflation. Opposition spokesmen contend that the budget has taken back from the public $2 for every $1 given in the previous budget, that the percentages of increase announced by the government on certain goods will be further increased by producers' costs which will result in a further increase in the cost of living, and that the total tax for the year will be $640 million and not $245 million, as announced in the budget. Opposition spokesmen will claim that living standards have declined in the past year, that there was a reduction in real earnings
The Budget-Mr. McWilliam and that the true deficit figure is $835 million and not $617 million, as announced in the budget.
As government and opposition members take part in this debate comparisons will go on and on. Many speakers present a story on the budget items which they have derived from research and which they feel gives a true picture. However, in many cases with the human element being in the forefront guiding the thoughts along certain channels, factors that are pleasant predominate while factors that do not suit the taste are dropped.
I am of the opinion that most hon. members of this house are far from being experts on government financing. I am one of those. This being the case, I do not intend to dwell upon the financial aspects of the budget except for a few comments. Everyone understands what taxes are and what increased taxes, hidden or otherwise, mean to us as individuals in our everyday lives. We know that if taxes are increased we must increase our personal income to provide and maintain our present standard of living. People do not like to cut back their standard of living, especially in peacetime, and therefore will look for opportunities to increase their income when the cost of living rises. As these costs increase they look for matching increases in family revenue.
It sounds very patriotic to say that Canadians must work harder and produce more to keep their economy buoyant. Canadians generally speaking are prepared to work harder to improve the economy of the country, to provide for their families a good standard of living, to work toward the accumulation of holdings that will provide security in the future, to provide education for their children and to assist their children in getting established.
I wish I could share the optimism of those who state that the Atlantic provinces are on the doorstep of economic and industrial expansion. The only apparent industrial expansion in that area is in the city of Saint John, New Brunswick. The other areas of those provinces are in the main very depressed. The Newfoundland cod fishing industry is in dire straits. The maritime lumber industry both in terms of export and import is labouring under the hardship of falling prices and decreasing markets. The maritime coal industry is in a most precarious state and income from maritime farming is away below the Canadian average. Many sectors of our base metal industry have closed down.
Immediate action toward the improvement of trade policies is vital and essential. Major government projects that will provide lasting

The Budget-Mr. McWilliam benefits must be undertaken. The government must provide the opportunity to increase trade and seek by other means to keep alive the very lifeline of the provinces on the Atlantic coast and thus pave the way for an improved economy.
Shortly after confederation the maritimes fell out of step with Upper Canada. The great contribution they made went to the benefit of Upper Canada and in later years to western Canada. The maritimes received little in return. The wider benefits that are the inherent right of the maritime and Atlantic provinces never became a reality.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we adjourned for the dinner recess at six o'clock I was commencing to make some remarks with regard to confederation and how it affected the maritime provinces. I said that shortly after confederation the maritimes fell out of step with Upper Canada and that the great contributions that were made by the people of the maritimes at that time and in the years following confederation went chiefly to the benefit of Upper Canada and in later years to western Canada. The sacrifices made by our forefathers in the maritimes did not bring about the good results held out by confederation. The visions held out which brought about union and prompted great sacrifices and toil by our forefathers in the maritimes were not realized.
In a great many respects the maritime provinces today, on a comparative basis with the rest of Canada, are in a much less favourable position than they were in the period prior to and immediately following confederation. I feel that the maritimes paid the price of union and their inherent rights were not recognized down through the years. Throughout the years many of our maritime leaders have promoted the view that the maritimes should break away from confederation. I do not think this is a solution and I certainly do not hold this view. There are no better Canadians, than the people who live in the maritime provinces.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: British Columbia.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will include other parts of Canada. Maritimers wish to remain full-fledged Canadians, these descendants of the Scots, the French, the Irish and the English

who are proud to call themselves Canadian. In my opinion the solution lies in the proper recognition by the federal government, proper recognition as of right as the first step and as subsequent action is necessary to bring about the balanced economy which we believe is so necessary for the provinces by the Atlantic ocean.
I am sure that Atlantic province members of both parties share these views and desires and in their own respective and limited ways they are trying to bring this about. The onus is upon the federal cabinet members from these four provinces. Theirs is the task to convince their cabinet colleagues that action must be taken. Their provincial differences, if any exist, must be resolved and they must present a united front before their cabinet colleagues, a united Atlantic provinces front.
The federal cabinet ministers from the maritimes, and I say this sincerely, are doing a good job as heads of the departments of veterans affairs, fisheries and national revenue, and we in the maritimes think it is unfortunate that one of them is not Minister of Trade and Commerce. As the chief spokesmen for the Atlantic provinces they have a most important job to do, the task of bringing a balanced economy to the provinces they represent. In their efforts toward this end they will receive the support of all Atlantic coast members and the support of all groups and people in the area.
Many and varied suggestions to improve conditions are a matter of record. The Atlantic provinces economic council, is working toward this end. Other groups have presented views and are anxious to assist in the field work. Bold and imaginative action is required. Efforts of the type made in varying degrees in the past will not be sufficient in my opinion. A better, a wider, a more comprehensive over-all plan is needed. A more practical and realistic plan must be put in action. This is the appeal I make particularly to the Atlantic provinces cabinet ministers.
While it is realized that all parts of Canada cannot be on an absolute par, nevertheless no part of this great country should be lagging behind the average level to the extent that the Atlantic provinces are. It has been said often that the greatest export of the maritimes is brains. Lack of opportunity has been the reason why our better educated and highly skilled young people leave the provinces of their birth. Opportunities are vital to keep them at home where they can make great contributions to their respective provinces.

Because the area in square miles is much smaller than other provinces and because the population figures are lower should not work to their disadvantage when consideration is being given at the federal level toward improving the economy of the Atlantic provinces. Because we have only three Atlantic provinces ministers as heads of departments of government and one minister without portfolio should not weaken our case at the federal cabinet level.
There are only three Liberals from the maritimes, all from the neighbouring constituencies of Gloucester, Northumberland-Miramichi and Kent on the east coast of New Brunswick. They have been referred to as the three members from the Gaza strip. There are five Liberal members from Newfoundland who I am sure join with all the Conservative members from the Atlantic provinces in the hope that a program involving a planned economy will be undertaken to improve the conditions which I have outlined generally in my speech.
Budgets will come and budgets will go. Budgets will be drafted by the department's financial experts and the minister of finance of the government of the day. Taxes may be increased or may be decreased, all of which has a bearing on the country at the particular time. But what is more important at this time, more important than the present budget, to the people of the Atlantic provinces is an uplift in our economy, the providing of additional opportunities for our people to make the uplift a reality and provide security for the future of these people, descendants of the pioneers of our nation who have a deep sense of loyalty and responsibility and who are still prepared to make sacrifices to build a bigger and better Canada. They only ask for the opportunity to keep on making contributions to our Canadian way of life on an equal basis with the Canadian average. I trust, Mr. Speaker, that any efforts that are made will be crowned with success and the inherent rights under consideration will at last be ours.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great privilege for me to have the opportunity to address myself to the current budget debate. It is a debate in relation to a budget which in its forthrightness asks sacrifices from those who can sacrifice. It is a budget which considers those people who must be considered under present economic and social conditions.
During the past elections many Canadians supported the present government because our party told the people of Canada that they would bring government back to the people and the people back to the government, to
The Budget-Mr. Grafftey the House of Commons, where it ought to be. I feel sure that this is borne out by the fact the Canadian people today are taking a greater interest than they ever have in exactly what is happening in this House of Commons, and by the fact that the budget now under discussion has kept faith with the people.
I noticed that at the start of this budget debate the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquit-lam (Mr. Regier) referred to the fact that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) told the Canadian people there was no reason to have fear. Then he read into this statement all kinds of ulterior motives. I say the very reason that the Minister of Finance made such a statement was because of the doom, gloom and pessimism which has been preached by opposition members. I have attended this debate quite regularly since it began and I have heard one opposition member after another criticize the high expenditures. However, I have not heard one suggestion as to what expenditures they would cut. Would they cut the increased old age pensions? Would they cut the increased hospital insurance? All these measures have resulted in increased expenditures. Not one suggestion have they offered to the Canadian House of Commons during this debate with regard to the cutting of expenditures.
I have not been surprised. This opposition is what I call a Hamlet opposition, "To be or not to be". They have a very uncanny knack of falling on both sides of every question that is brought to the floor of this house. You know, sir, they did almost the impossible. I think I witnessed the impossible being done by the Liberal party on the floor of this house recently. It was almost as rare as a triple play in baseball. During the Newfoundland debate they actually fell on three sides of the question.
During the budget debate this morning I noticed that the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) mentioned the unions. He was talking about labour unions in relation to their international affiliations. When he mentioned unions I could not help but think of a remark he made during the closing days of the last session. I shall show you why I feel the remark he made had something to do with unions. He said that the C.C.F. party would go to the next election with increased money muscles. I asked myself exactly how they would get bigger money muscles for the next election. I think, Mr. Speaker, I have the answer. Oh, I know they are going to say that once these things come about there will be freedom at the local level of the unions. I have heard that argument before. I will tell the C.C.F. how they think

The Budget-Mr. Grafftey -they will not-they are going to get increased money muscles for the next election. The only way they could do it would be by deductions from the pockets of workingmen and women who never have and never will support the C.C.F. socialist movement in this country.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Port Arthur mentioned they might be there tonight, but I cannot see him in the house, either.
We, as Canadians, can be rightfully proud of one thing and that is since the days of confederation we have encouraged and nurtured a classless society founded on the truest type of democratic principles. I know how hard this is for my friends away yonder in the C.C.F. to appreciate. They would not like this, I know, because one only had to listen to their leader on budget night to realize that that party has its own little divide and rule game to play. I can tell the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) that the Canadian people will never tolerate or be drawn into this type of bitter "chip on the shoulder" warfare.
I realize that tradition designates a fair latitude of discussion on both the budget debate and the throne speech debate. It is for this reason that this evening I should like to relate to the House of Commons some of the impressions and some of the observations I made recently as an observer of the last session of the United Nations general assembly. I can assure you that I have been duly warned about the dangers and pitfalls which face a freshman member of parliament who plunges into the intricacies of foreign affairs. I can equally assure you and the house, sir, that 1 do not intend to go into any farflung interpretation of international conditions. I was merely an observer, and I merely have observations to offer.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to offer my deepest and most sincere condolences to the family of our late secretary of state for external affairs, the Hon. Sidney Smith. As a young man, I had the great honour and privilege of serving under his guidance at the United Nations. Again, Mr. Speaker, I offer my sincere condolences to his family, and I bow to his memory.
(Text):
Basically, the United Nations is performing a pretty straightforward function, but perhaps we all have a tendency to look upon it as a bit of a mystery, even though we have


a general appreciation of how it works and even though something is usually written about it each day in our newspapers. The United Nations today is performing a role and functions which were not clearly visualized during the early days of San Francisco. Like so many people in Canada, and in this House of Commons, I have read a great many reports emanating from the United Nations during the postwar years. I had a general appreciation of how the various councils and agencies were set up, but never did I feel that I had a real insight into the basic meaning of this world organization. As one columnist put it to me, "The world today needs a meeting place and this is it."
I readily admit that seven weeks is too short a time in which to gain a complete insight into many of the complex problems which face the security council and the general assembly but it is not necessarily too short a time in which to realize that situated within this building on the East river are to be found ideals and principles which just must work in the world of today. Inevitably [DOT]-and I say, sir, unfortunately-the political aspect of the United Nations gets most of the publicity.
I think most of us here today realize that when something goes wrong in the world it is bound to end up in the security council or the general assembly. Much public criticism is often levelled in the direction of the United Nations because, after endless talk, charges and countercharges, often no solutions are reached and resolutions passed are often flagrantly violated by member countries. Yet I suggest that in the United Nations we are dealing with problems which are as old as man, problems which the United Nations itself did not create but which are aired and dealt with by nations and men with all their faults, both good and bad. As man does not always live up to the principles of his religion, so nations and men do not always live up to the principles of the United Nations and its charter. But this does not mean that we should destroy the institution which, as I have said before, is so often merely a mirror for nations, men and their collective behaviour.
(Translation):
It is often said that not enough attention is paid to the hard day to day work of the United Nations. The work they accomplish for children, refugees and underdeveloped countries of the world is so important. Such agencies as the World Health Organization work without letup. Let us look for a moment at one example of international cooperation: how a letter or a parcel can be delivered, in a very short time, to any corner of the world? You address your letter,

put a stamp on it, mail it in your own town and often, after quite a lot of handling, it rapidly gets to destination. This is not done by some miracle, but because of a continuous international co-operation.
(Text):
Mr. Speaker, in relation to the United Nations I have yet another brief observation to make and it is this. I felt that many of the member countries wished to remain uncommitted to either the east or the west. It is so important that we attempt to capture their imagination by good example. At the same time I feel that too much public emphasis should not be placed on a struggle to line these countries up with the western camp, as so many of the middle powers have their own destinies to follow. When parents sometimes separate and quarrel in public over the custody of their children, frequently the latter back away and seek their own home and way of life. When I say that we should capture their imagination by good example, and while the historical doctrine of the two swords separates church from state, we in the west should never be too shy to tell the communist countries in clear and emphatic terms that our political, social and economic orders are founded on eternal religious principles. For this reason it seems so extremely important that we do not limit our debate with the communist bloc to the economic level, even while the so-called cold war has taken on characteristics of an economic nature.
It seemed that the citizens of many of the member countries at the United Nations had seen tyranny at first hand. They deeply feel and deeply believe in the principles and ideals embodied in this institution. For this very reason I think it is extremely important that we as Canadians, living in a most privileged land, never look upon this international institution merely as an intellectual proposition; for before too long I personally sense that the authority of the general assembly and the security council will have real teeth in it. While I dwelt on this thought my mind wandered back to the early days of parliamentary history, and I wondered exactly what Westminster looked like at that time. Then I realized that, while the United Nations oftentimes passed resolution after resolution which were often openly and flagrantly violated by member countries, they perhaps here were evolving procedural customs and practices which ultimately would form the basis of a new type of body.
I listened with great interest to the fine speech delivered in this house yesterday by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe). After listening to his speech I realized that, in a realistic fashion, we might
The Budget-Mr. Grafftey be obliged to avoid calling it a world government; undoubtedly, we shall be obliged to avoid calling it a world government. But nevertheless, I feel that in the not too distant future the security council and the general assembly will have greater teeth in it. Admittedly the present voting and veto system leave much to be desired. But this state of affairs is not necessarily permanent, and no doubt patience and future demands will dictate change.
Another lasting impression that I took home with me relates to the secretary general himself. One could not help but be impressed by the energy, the integrity and the vigour of this great man. I think all hon. members of the Canadian House of Commons were more than interested to note that he acted for and on behalf of the United Nations in the Middle East dispute. One might easily say that the secretary general acted as a negotiating force. I can only add that as long as men of the integrity and the character of Mr. Hammarskjold occupy this high position of public service, it should prove to be a most interesting and useful experiment.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians should be rightfully proud of the part being placed by Canada at the United Nations. It has often been said that under modern conditions the middle and the smaller powers have a role of definite importance to play. As has been said so often both inside and outside of this house by myself and many other hon. members, Canada herself is in a unique position, often interpreting the old world to the new and the new world to the old. This should never mean, though, that we do not have our own well-defined stand on any major issue. Yet, when the major powers become deadlocked, it is often the smaller and the middle powers which come up with a solution. I am sure that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) is aware of these circumstances. As one Swedish correspondent said to me down in New York, "Small countries do not necessarily mean small ideas". As the head of the British delegation mentioned to some of the younger observers from the Canadian delegation down in New York, after our late secretary of state for external affairs had made his intervention in the political committee on the disarmament debate, "That was a fine speech by your secretary of state for external affairs; he said so many things that are better said by you than by us".
Circumstances offer us a peacemaking role which is often denied the larger powers, and while they gain much of the publicity at the United Nations, no country remains unaffected by world events nor can remain aloof

The Budget-Mr. Grafftey from the current interplay of international politics. I repeat, that the very forces which cemented and created Canadian confederation can help us play a most significant role today on the international stage. I am sure that hon. members in all parties will agree when I ask, what other country has had our extremely interesting history of dominion-provincial relations? I am certainly sure that all members of all parties will agree that dominion-provincial conferences have been and continue to be conferences which must be approached with a high degree of understanding compromise. I repeat that these qualities well equip Canada to play her role on the international scene.
With this in mind, we should always realize that compromise should never be overstressed under present conditions. I think all of us here today would readily admit that what I refer to as the compromise spirit has many beneficial characteristics; but it also has characteristics of which I, in all sincerity, feel we should be aware. Admittedly, all confederate powers must approach their legislative functions with a spirit of compromise, and Canada is no exception to this rule. But in my opinion Canada has other distinct historical and current characteristics which add to what I call this compromise spirit.
Second, there is the above-mentioned go-between function on the international level; and third-I know I will be accused of having a partisan spirit when I say this- there was the long period of 22 years of Liberal rule where pragmatic compromise often keynoted the activities of a party which had long since abandoned its principles. So often it seemed to me that the architects of dullness misjudged the temper of our nation and its ability to absorb direction in its leadership. To know our strength is to know our history.
I make these remarks about compromise because it is so terribly important under present international conditions that Canada, on the international scene, does not take on a cool, aloof look of spiritless self-satisfaction. But I feel that under the present administration this can never happen. I have often said in the house, and I say it again here tonight, that under the present government the new spirit of Pan-Canadianism has united this country as it has never been united before. I say that this feeling of strength gives us a more united and strong look on the international scene, thus always assuring our allies exactly where we stand.
Sir, on my last day at the United Nations it was not very difficult to return home to Canada with a feeling of real and deep faith in this important world body. As I passed

along the corridors outside the general assembly hall I passed by men and women who had dedicated a great part of their lives to the important work of this body, men and women who realize that, in this short period of history, man is faced with a task which must be lived up to, which must be challenged. I returned home to a country which is a comparatively young country; a young member of the family of nations living together on the banks of the East river. Yet to me it seems to be a most welcome member, a member which should bring those qualities of optimism and imagination to a living room which is sometimes sad, and to a household which too often loses its sense of humour.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not going to be like the hon. member who has just taken his seat and speak during the budget debate about a subject which at this particular time has very little to do with the budget. I was wondering if there was any reason why he steered his speech away from the budget into other channels. I suppose there have been many names given to this particular budget according to the way it appeals to those who have read and paid attention to it. I would call it the pay-off budget. It is the budget that has demanded of Canada payment for the election promises and the wild spending of the present Conservative party. In the last two years we have danced the dance and now we must pay the fiddler. But I was rather interested in the way this budget debate began.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You fellows are expert fiddlers anyway.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You will have your chance when your time comes, and you will probably steer away from the budget too, and I do not blame you. As I was saying, I was interested in the way the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) came into the chamber to deliver his budget speech. I thought the carnation with its artificial colouring was conspicuous by its absence. I thought the reading stand had been bared of the usual blue velvet, but I suppose the time had come when the Minister of Finance was no longer going to handle the people of Canada with velvet; this was going to be a harder budget. We, I suppose, have been able to see this budget in the light of the many promises which have been made over the last two election campaigns. I am not going into a long speech reiterating these; that has already been done. But we can see the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), for example, flitting across this country in the spring of 1957 telling the people that they were overtaxed by $500 million, that each family was

overtaxed by $120 a year, that Canadian people were overtaxed by $30 for every man, woman and child in the country. Yes, we can see the Prime Minister saying all this, and we can also see him telling what services were going to be given under his government if he were elected. We can see him standing up and telling the people who listened to him, "Give us a chance and we will show you."
We have seen in this particular budget that it is impossible to provide more benefits and increase the spending of the government without the time coming when these bills have to be paid. But I suppose these are election promises which, according to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), are not very sacred anyway. But if one could judge from recent happenings I might say that even contracts which have been laid on the table of the House of Commons are not very sacred either. So it appears we are now being ruled by a government which rules by expediency, although before the election of 1957 they were the champions of rule by law and of the dignity of office.
In former budget discussions we heard a lot about the vision. This year it has scarcely been mentioned. I am reminded of the professor who was trying to explain to one of his students how it is possible in the English language to have two words which normally mean the same thing but which, placed in different contexts, may mean something entirely opposite. And as an illustration he said, "Take the words 'vision' and 'sight'. At the college dance, the girl you had was a vision and the one I had was a sight." I think that the Tory vision has now gravitated into a definite sight.
I should like to pass on to one of the aspects of our financial affairs which in the last three or four years has occupied the attention of many people. I want to speak for a minute or so on interest rates. I do not intend to define interest rates, because every hon. member will know what interest rates are and how they are calculated. I am sure all hon. members will all know how important the interest rate is to the people of this country, particularly to provincial governments and to municipal governments. We have heard many fears expressed in the past about the difficult times ahead for provincial governments, municipalities and other borrowers because the interest rate on borrowed money was so high. I listened to the Minister of Finance when he spoke as a member of the opposition on August 11, 1956, as reported on page 7462 of Hansard. He said this:
The effect of these repeated increases in interest rates-five in the period of one year-
The Budget-Mr. Batten
May I stress the word "five"?
-has been a tremendous increase in the burdens cast upon provincial governments with respect to their borrowings and upon municipal governments with respect to their borrowings and upon business, and punishing losses upon the holders of Canada's obligations.
These were the words of the Minister of Finance, as he is now, on August 11, and at the time he was speaking the interest rate was 3.25 per cent. The hon. gentleman has been witnessing over the last three months some very significant increases in these interest rates although the Conservative party pledged during the election campaign that they would be reduced. Not only did the hon. gentleman's party pledge to reduce them, but they also took credit for reducing them, and I say to the Conservative party today: if you are going to take credit for reducing the interest rate I fear you will also have to take the blame for raising it. If you take credit for the drop, you will also have to take the blame for the rise. Listen to the Prime Minister speaking at Calgary on March 14, 1958 as reported in the Winnipeg Tribune of March 15. The report reads:
He claimed that interest rates had fallen sharply as a result of government action since last June from a high of 4.33 per cent to 2.89 per cent in recent weeks.
If the Prime Minister thought that 4.33 was a high rate, I suggest he should compare that with the rate last week.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And it was higher yesterday.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Prime Minister went on to speak in Selkirk, Manitoba, on March 7, 1958, as reported in the Toronto Telegram of March 18. After claiming that the government had eased the tight money situation, he went on to say:
This has been done by releasing $300 million for new housing, launching a vast public works program and by reducing taxes.
Incidentally, I wonder where that public works program went to. Then, in Halifax, on March 24, 1958, as reported in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald:
Referring to finances, Mr. Diefenbaker said his government reversed the "tight money policy of the Liberals". Interest rates had been decreased from 4.3 per cent to 2.8 per cent. As a result of the $300 million provided for housing loans there were more housing starts on homes "for average Canadians" than ever before.
Yet despite the promises which were made in 1958, we find that the interest rate today is higher than it has ever been before, and if we look at the rates since January 7, 1959 we shall find that there has been a gradual increase from a rate of 3.5 per cent to a figure which, last week, was 4.67 per cent. Surely if there were grave disadvantages for the

The Budget-Mr. Batten provinces and the municipalities, as predicted two years ago, when interest rates were lower than 4 per cent, those disadvantages are present today in a much more acute form. Here is a case of just another promise which was made to the people of Canada and forgotten after the balloting was over.
May I now proceed for a moment to a discussion of the gross national product. The Minister of Finance began his budget by explaining how he thought the Canadian people were prepared for an increase in taxes, and he went on to condition even the members of the House of Commons on those lines. He talked about the flexibility of budgets, and so on; in fact I thought at times that the budget which the minister was reading was a treatise on flexibility by inflexible Fleming. At any rate, the hon. gentleman went on to forecast an increase of 7 per cent in the gross national product, provided, of course, that prices remain stable. I think there are many people across this country who doubt that in the coming year there can be an increase of 7 per cent in the gross national product.
Earlier in the year, the Minister of Finance predicted a gradual improvement in the position, or a gradual growth in the gross national product, and I think he was right in this expectation. But I do not think that an increase of 7 per cent at this particular time, with stable prices, could be considered as normal or steady growth. I believe that is exaggerating. After all, a recovery of 7 per cent in the gross national product very nearly approaches boom conditions; that was the size of the growth in 1956. I think we have to bear in mind that this recession has been something more than a pause; that it has dug deeper into our economy. I believe that from here on we are never going to have conditions which will be quite the same as before. Our economy has been readjusted because of this recession, mild as it was. These recessions always have an effect on the economy of the country in which they occur, and here in Canada, particularly, where we are so dependent on foreign trade, it is difficult to see how a recession coming at a time when there is also a recession in other countries could not have a very serious effect upon the economy. Other countries are expanding. Other countries are making efforts to capture new markets, and to the extent to which they succeed a new problem is created for a country such as Canada which must depend for its livelihood on trade.
Take as an example Canadian exports to the United States. These do not reflect the recovery that we might have expected or the recovery which I think is taking place in the United States. Let me give the house one case with which I feel I am familiar; I refer to

the newsprint industry. The demand for newsprint in the United States for the first quarter of 1959 increased by 4.4 per cent, but Canadian exports to the United States were down by 6 per cent. This was not due to a decrease in production in Canada, because the decrease in the production of newsprint in Canada amounted to only 1.7 per cent.
I do think the minister's forecast of a 7 per cent increase in the gross national product is somewhat ambitious. In 1958, for example, the increase in the gross national product was 2.5 per cent over 1957 but the larger part of this was taken up by increases in prices. In actual fact the increase in the gross national product for 1958 over 1957 was less than 1 per cent.
One might go on and make reference to some more figures. By volume, 1958 was less than 1 per cent over 1957. In 1957 there was very little change over 1956 and for the period 1947 to 1958 the average growth in the gross national product was 4 per cent. It does indeed appear that the minister's forecast was a little high and yet it is the forecast on which he bases his figures for the coming year.
In talking about the gross national product let us have a look at the corporation tax. The corporation tax was increased by 3 percentage points which means that the actual tax to be paid by corporations that make a profit of more than $25,000 for the year 1959 will be increased by approximately 6 per cent over that of 1958. This means that the main sources of employment are being taxed rather highly. Modern plants and modern equipment are needed to produce in Canada products at a price acceptable in the foreign markets. If we are going to tax our corporations too highly it will mean that the price at which the products we produce will be sold will be unacceptable in the markets of the world.
In 1958, the corporation tax was about 5 per cent lower than in 1957. In 1957 it was lower than in 1956 but there were gains in 1955 and 1956. When we look at the fact that the corporation tax is decreasing we must ask ourselves this question: Are we levying increased taxes on a decreasing return? I think that is perhaps what we are trying to do here. We must realize that our corporations produce the goods we sell. While I think the corporation tax is decreasing, I have no doubt in my mind about the Canadian potential. I believe we have a great potential for production in the future. However, we have in this country a great deal of old plant facilities and old plant equipment. I believe the time has come when industrial Canada should take a good look at itself and compare its capacity to increase with its present

potential. In the years that lie ahead this will be a matter of great importance to our country.
I wish now to refer briefly to federal-provincial relations. Hon. members will remember that this is one of the topics that occupied the attention of many of those who traversed this country in 1957 and in the campaign of 1958. We will remember that promises were made in 1957 to the effect that a federal-provincial conference would be called immediately if the Diefenbaker party were elected. Well, it was elected and the conference was called, not immediately but in November. I was present at that conference, at least the public part of it. For all that was done the premiers of the provinces might just as well have stayed home and sent in their submissions by mail. They rose and read their presentations to the conference and proceeded to go back home to their respective provinces having been given the promise that they would meet again in January. They did not meet in January. Instead of a meeting being called the premiers were the recipients of the notorious telegrams sent by the Minister of Finance in December stating what was going to be done and saying, in effect, "You must take it or leave it".
We saw a reflection of this same attitude in the throne speech. It contained no plan for arriving at some satisfactory solution to all the problems that now exist between the federal government and the provinces. Let me say immediately that the government has given a great deal of assistance to the provinces including the maritimes. I will be one of the first to admit that. My criticism of the government's attitude is that the assistance it has given the provinces and particularly the maritimes has not been the result of general policy but rather the result of a piecemeal operation which so characterizes the present administration.
I believe we have reached a time when, if these problems are going to be solved, a federal-provincial conference must be called. But I suggest that this government is not going to call such a conference at this time. My own province has some extremely serious problems in this respect but I shall wait for a proper occasion to make my specific comments concerning these matters. I trust, however, that the Minister of Finance does not think that reducing the excise tax on artificial bait and lures is any substitution for the fulfilment of term 29 of the articles of union.
In conclusion may I suggest that the supporters of this budget have been arguing, in effect, that it is just right for the present financial situation. I must confess there is some truth in that position, but let me hasten
The Budget-Mr. Keays to add that the present financial situation with which this government finds itself confronted is of its own making. Members of the government have gone out around the country and have made promises to the people. They came into parliament, formed the government and proceeded to spend wildly. Now that they have spent the bills must be paid and they are demanding that the Canadian people pay increased taxes in order to bail them out.
I believe that the Canadian people will accept this budget resignedly because they believe nothing else can be done under the present circumstances. I am also of the opinion, however, that many people across the country will know that the present financial situation is one the government voluntarily got itself into.
