speechtext:
As I rise to take part in this debate, I wish first of all to convey to this house the gratitude and appreciation of the people of Gaspe, where I have the honour of being mayor, concerning the recent announcement that Her Gracious Majesty will visit that town on June 21 next. The itinerary as announced was very welcome. Recently a dispatch has been sent to Her Gracious Majesty expressing on behalf of our town good wishes for a safe voyage and expressing the eagerness of our townspeople to receive her.
It is interesting to note that when the royal couple visit our great country they will first pay a visit to the youngest province of Canada and then the oldest. When I say the oldest, Mr. Speaker, I refer to the year 1534 when that famous French explorer, Jacques Cartier, by the act of erecting a cross took possession of this country in the name of God and his country. Throughout the annals of history Gaspe has always been described as the birthplace of civilization in Canada and I was somewhat disturbed by the fact that at the celebrations in honour of Champlain in Quebec city last year they attributed to themselves the honour of being the birthplace of Canada. It was at Gaspe. With this in mind I wish to convey to the house the appreciation and gratitude of our people at receiving her.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I wonder whether the hon. gentleman would permit a question?

The Budget-Mr. Keays

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will permit a carload of questions as soon as I have finished my remarks. I should like to speak for my constituents and express their heartfelt thanks to the government for acceding to the request for an economic and physical survey of the Magdalen islands. This was undertaken by the government in the fall of 1958 and I must say that it was a thorough investigation. It proved that the Magdalen islands have been forgotten and I trust sincerely that when the study has been completed these people will be given a chance to win the battle they have been fighting since 1653, the battle between man and the sea, the battle for the right of survival of the people of these islands and the right to earn what they need for their existence. I am quite sure that when these studies have been completed these islands will be given the harbours and fishing facilities needed for the survival of the people.
As I have mentioned, Mr. Speaker, these islands have for long been forgotten. The history of the islands dates back to 1653 when Nicolas Denys took possession of same as a favour from his government and since that time the people have been engaged in the battle to which I have referred. I should like to refer to an article which appeared in a local newspaper, Le Phare, in October, 1948, and which reads as follows:
(Translation):
The cove provides so little security that people have to get up on very stormy nights to go and pull the boats ashore, and there are only 30 of these boats left in the bay. Fishermen are getting discouraged and try to find a more stable way of earning a living elsewhere. Our two seaports are only so in name: They are Havre Aubert and Cap aux Meules. They are in need of dredging and of some construction work: breakwaters and jetties, so that ships of higher tonnage might find shelter there. Some coastal communities, which have neither our population figure nor our volume of business have well-organized seaports. The project is therefore practicable. Our requests are reasonable.
(Text):
It then goes on to say, Mr. Speaker, (Translation):
Magdalen islanders are hoping that the federal authorities will one day favourably consider their requests.
The same paper wrote in December 1948:
If that field were under provincial jurisdiction, there would be action and no mere promises. (Text):
I then read the ideas of Robert Rumilly, a great historian and one interested in the problems of the Magdalen islands: (Translation):
And that is true. The federal government is as indifferent and negligent with regard to the isles as was the provincial government until 1936. We would let them off if they did for the islands a tenth of what the provincial administration did for us. Let me write down all my thoughts, which
[Mr. Pickersgill.l

have been confirmed by 13 years of experience in Ottawa. The federal government has jurisdiction on the sea fisheries of all provinces, except Quebec. So that the federal treasury, fed by Quebec taxes, looks after the maintenance of fisheries in all provinces who have any, except those in Quebec. The federal administration being freed from that load should as a compensation take more interest in our ports which are still under its jurisdiction. The victims of this federal sulking are the fishermen.
(Text):
It is therefore apparent, Mr. Speaker, that the Magdalen islands have long been neglected and as a result of the study undertaken and a realization of the needs the government has already undertaken the construction of a large wharf at Grindstone island, the construction of a wharf at Amherst island, commonly called Havre-Aubert, these facilities permitting the fishermen to approach the fish processing plants. I am sure that the study undertaken by the government will prove that the people of the Magdalen islands have long been forgotten and that it is time to realize their needs.
New transportation facilities are required and subsidies to encourage the establishment of such facilities. Although the present air service is quite adequate, unfortunately the freight rate is rather high for the transportation of fish by air. For your information, Mr. Speaker, the first steamboat to ply between the islands and Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island started to do so in 1876. The first telegraph line was installed in 1880, but unfortunately broke down in 1910. The numerous requests which were made to this government at the time for transportation facilities fell upon deaf ears.
It was then that the mayor of House Harbour or Havre-aux-Maisons, Alcide Gau-dette, thought of one method of transportation. He arranged a barrel or cask in which he placed the mail going to the relatives of these people in the United States, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and the Matapedia valley. These were the relatives of the deported Acadians. Then, on this barrel he placed a little white flag to represent the spirit of the people in those islands. Some days later he set this new mode of transportation afloat and left it to the will of the open seas. It left on January 8, 1910 and on February 12 this barrel landed on Cape Breton island. In the barrel there was a letter addressed to the then postmaster general, Hon. Rodolphe Lemieux, which said: "If you cannot send a reply by boat, send it in this barrel".
The result of this communication was that in March of that year a steamboat left Sydney carrying mail. It is noteworthy also, that in 1911 with the advent of the Borden government the first Marconi station was

installed on the Magdalen islands. The people of the island were then granted a special privilege from the fall until the spring of sending 2,000 words per week free of charge. This was the beginning of regular transportation between the islands and the mainland.
It is easy to conceive, that everything was not rosy for these brave fishermen. What they claim today, as I have already mentioned, is the right of survival and the right to a share in the general economy of our country. We have heard a great deal of criticism from the opposition of this budget. I would not dare say that much of it was of a substantial nature, but rather seemed to follow the present policy of the opposition of criticizing without making constructive suggestions. They seem to be endeavouring to instil in the minds of Canadians a state of despondency. If only this mode of criticism could be left aside and the opposition would make a volte-face, we might hear something concrete and beneficial.
We hear repeated references to inflation and recession. I should like to refer to what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) said as recorded on page 35 of Hansard for January 19, 1959:
While we were in office, Liberal fiscal, monetary and economic policies were sound, steady-and steadiness is pretty important-flexible and successful. They made it possible for this country to combine startling economic expansion and reasonable monetary stability.
We know, that the contrary is true. Reports received from many financial institutions indicate that our economy is more stable today than it has been during the last few years. This opinion, is shared by many of the financial institutions in this country. Although we are aware of the dangers of inflation, much of this is of a chronic nature. The Minister of Finance has brought in a budget which is aimed at combatting inflation and reducing its dangers. This budget is very important and, as evidence will prove later, was brought in as a medium of attacking inflation, keeping in mind the genuine recovery of our economy. This, in itself, is very commendable, is good business practice and logic.
The Minister of Finance has endeavoured to further narrow the deficit and, as he mentioned in his speech, has brought in a budget designed to foster recovery. It is conceded that the mere statement made by the Minister of Finance will not, in itself, be a cure-all for the inflationary dangers, but is rather merely the first step provided by the government to relieve the dangers.
I should like to bring to the attention of this house the fact that inflation is not the sole concern of government but of every individual taxpayer in Canada. A few minutes
The Budget-Mr. Keays ago I mentioned that first public reaction to the presentation of the budget was probably doubtful. However, after the business consultants, analysts and critics had a chance of studying the proposed actions contained in this budget, they were pleased and commended the minister for his courage in facing reality and giving us a budget commensurate with the needs of the day.
Mr. A. C. Ashforth, president of the Toronto-Dominion bank, and president of the Canadian chamber of commerce, is quoted in the Winnipeg Free Press as follows:
I believe balanced budget, or close to one, would improve the bond market and general business. I personally was not surprised at the Increase in income taxes to meet the current situation. However, I do feel that income taxes are too high on a long term basis for a young developing country like Canada.
We cannot expect the government to lower taxes if we, the public, are constantly asking them to do more and more for us.
Every penny the government spends has to come out of the pockets of the taxpayers. There is no other source. I am pleased to see the minister of finance is optimistic about the volume of this year's business.
Mr. Laurent Lauzier in an article in La Presse of Montreal of April 11 has this to say:
(Translation):
The federal budget continues to give rise to many comments, especially among businessmen and, above all, among income tax experts. The first hours of reflection and consideration having elapsed, the actual objectives aimed at by the government in its budgetary resolutions, introduced Thursday night by the Hon. Donald Fleming, Minister of Finance, are better grasped.
In financial quarters there seems to be general agreement-
(Text):
I should like hon. members of this house to note this.
(Translation):
In financial quarters there seems to be general agreement about the necessity of the tax increases announced by the government. It is generally believed that the increases provided are not high enough to hamper the economic recovery now in full swing.
(Text):
I have one more quotation coming from the income tax committee of the Chamber of Commerce which was presided over by Mr. Charles McLaughlin. He had this to say in an article in La Presse of Montreal of April 11:
(Translation):
The tax committee of the chamber of commerce, presided over by Mr. Charles McLaughlin, C.A., chief of the taxation division at the Canadian Industries Ltd., notes that the tax increase is slightly lower than could have been expected in the circumstances. He approves of the general attitude of the government, which seems to have looked for a middle course solution between a fight

The Budget-Mr. Keays
against inflation and a balanced budget. The committee notes also that the government is showing an obvious desire to protect the taxpayer, small or average, in restricting its income tax increases to higher income brackets and its sales tax increases to luxury articles.
(Text):
Last night, Mr. Speaker, I attended the closing meeting of the Canadian mining convention and I met a friend of mine who attended the luncheon on Tuesday of the chartered accountants and business administrators of the city of Montreal. He admitted that everyone was surprised that when the experts on administration and financial affairs spoke, every one of them said there was no other course to follow and that they endorsed the courage of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming).
It is noteworthy, Mr. Speaker, that when statements such as these are made we find that they come from people who have no political axe to grind. All hon. members know that the best interests of our form of government demand that those with authority to speak must give constructive criticism to legislative government so that the rights and concerns of all sections of our country are made known to the legislators. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) himself was well aware of this situation when speaking in Winnipeg last year to the Canadian Labour Congress. He then asked labour to hold the line with respect to demands for wage increases. Regrettably, such has not been the case, and in many instances labour has requested increases in revenue which were much to the detriment of the companies concerned.
There are those in this house sitting at our extreme right who have a well-known reaction to any announcements made in this house of government subsidies to farmers, industries or others. Whenever a statement is made that $40 million or $6 million or $2 million is to be made available to the public, they have but one common reaction: it is either peanuts or it is not enough. This group want bigger grants, bigger social security commitments and higher wages, with no concern for higher productivity.
Mr. Speaker, in order that a country can prosper, the corporations must make a profit and take out of their surplus the requirements for their expansion and future development. I do not say that all unions are in the same boat, because some have justly understood the problem and have heeded the warning of the Prime Minister. Labour in general has made a grand contribution to our development; but unfortunately there are still those who do not understand that increases in salary should also bring about increase in

productivity, in order thereby to keep our dollar value as stable as possible.
Mr. Speaker, may I interrupt this speech to say that the score is still 0-0 at the end of the second period.
On the other hand, we have those in our country who are the executives of large corporations and who have an important say in the directives given to industries. To many of these persons can be atributed the dangers in our economy. Too many after dinner speakers and social club speakers spend their time criticising government legislation without endeavouring in any way whatever to suggest any solution to the problems always confronting government and refusing to take an interest in their communities in so far as these problems affect the economy of our country. They deprive their communities, their province and their country of the gift of their talents. They fail to see the forest for the trees and miss a great opportunity to create better public relations to the benefit of their concerns.
Those who seem afraid of public life or who seem to look down upon those who take an active part in it will be well advised to reconsider their position and to realize that they owe a debt to their communities and to their country. Instead of staying away from public life and avoiding exposing themselves to criticism, they should think the matter over and, if possible, bring to their communities, as I have already mentioned, the gift of their talents.
I was very happy some time ago to read what another Gaspesian, Gratton O'Leary of the Ottawa Journal, when speaking at a luncheon meeting in the Chateau Laurier during the congress of the Ottawa insurance agents' association, had to say, and I quote:
Canada's business leaders sit "in the bleachers" and complain about the government but don't know what they are talking about because they take no active interest in public affairs. They sit in the bleachers. They talk loudly about inflation. But I don't see any of them telling us what should be done. Businessmen were calling at the same time for both lower taxes and a balanced budget.
Those who believe they are born to be sheep should endeavour to be shepherds and become the leaders of labour and industry and help those who take an active part in the business and financial problems of our Canadian economy. There is a place in Canada for everyone to be in the flock and not to be of those who eventually find themselves in the camp of those who oppose constitutional government, or even find themselves the leaders of such groups.
Before concluding, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to a speech made in this house by the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin) reported in Hansard at page 207. The hon. member referred to the infamous strike at

Murdochville. I am not going to defend Gaspe copper mines, nor am I going to defend Noranda mines, its president, vice-president or other officials. But I believe in all justice to those labourers who stayed on the job that they deserve to be defended, and I would like to tell this house that when they marched on Murdochville, 1,000 people from all over the province of Quebec, they found not 40 men back on the job but 675 people back on the job and willing to work. I say this because I live with the people and many have come to see me, crying and wondering what they should do. They were intimidated and afraid and would not return to work although they had five, six, seven or eight children to feed. They said, "What are we going to do? We are scared. We want to go back to work but are frightened". They were satisfied with the salaries paid and happy to work for a higher wage than they had ever earned before.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to mention how our Canada has come ahead from the days when Voltaire once described it as a few acres of snow, and relate the sentiment expressed by Mrs. Erich Neuhouser, a lady of German descent, who fears that Canadians are losing the pioneer spirit of their forefathers. This to some extent is true, and I believe that the alarm should now be sounded to revive this spirit, and with the example shown by many of our new Canadians give impetus to the development of this country and the vision as seen by this government.

speechtext:
Do you want me to be the leader? There is one thing I will be proud about to my dying day, and that is I was not, and never will be, a member of the Liberal party.
This attempt to substitute "Smallwoodism" for negativism does reflect the political dilemma of the party to my left and the situation which exists in Canada between the Tories and the Liberals. The Liberals know that their usual position on a seat on the fence a little left of centre does not exist any longer because the Tories have replaced them in it. As far as progressivism is concerned, the Tories are more progressive. So what can they do? They have gone just as far as they can go in a progressive direction, so now they say: we must go in the other direction; we must move to the position of being a reactionary group. At this point there comes into the picture a personage from Newfoundland, Premier Smallwood, hoping that with a policy of reassessment and re-examination the Liberal party might be built up to the position it once held; and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is paving the way for all this to take place.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Carving the way.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend says "carving the way". It may be a little more sanguinary but it does represent the quandary in which the Liberal party finds itself. I think we only have to make a comparison between the amendment put forward by the Liberals and the amendment to the amendment which we have proposed to be reminded of the differences which exist between our group and that which sits to my left. After all, our amendment, within the limited scope avail-


able, does recommend some positive, some constructive, some progressive action, and this is the role which the C.C.F. has always played even though we have never been in government. We have always led the way in progressive measures and in the introduction of constructive ideas. We do not complain because the Liberals over the years have stolen them, or that the Tories have stolen them. We wish to heaven they would take over the whole works and put it into effect because then we would have the kind of society we want.
One of our proposals deals with the question of instituting a capital gains tax. I think we are entitled to look at the condition which will develop in the future if we continue to be without a tax on capital gains while our neighbour to the south has imposed such a tax. First of all, such a tax on capital gains would provide a monetary incentive for the investment of United States capital in Canada and increase the influence exercised by the United States corporations in this country. That is one of the detrimental effects which such a situation would bring about. Another is that in some instances there would be a drain on the finances of Canada, because if a person or corporation from the United States invests in Canada, makes a capital gain and returns to the United States, such gain is subject to taxation by the United States authorities. In other words, funds which should be flowing into the coffers of the Canadian Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) are instead being diverted to the coffers of the United States treasury.
A third effect of such a situation is this: one of the by-products of the investment of United States money in Canada is a tendency to force up the exchange rate between the two countries which places us at a disadvantage in so far as world markets are concerned. It further places the Canadian taxpayer in an unfavourable position because he suffers at the hands of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) through having to raise additional money for taxes out of his own pockets. All this could be avoided if we had the capital gains tax we suggest. By his failure to institute this kind of tax, as we envisage it, the Minister of Finance has made the pro-Canadian type of speeches he used to make when in opposition sound extremely hollow. Indeed, his lack of action shows that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) spoke in a somewhat hypocritical fashion when he talked about United States buccaneers making piratical profits out of the pipe line stock deal, which was a capital gain.
Many of the unpleasant consequences which I have just mentioned would be overcome to a great extent if the minister

would only have the courage to introduce measures of the kind we have suggested in, apparently, what is to be one of his last actions as Minister of Finance before he moves to another office. I see a smile upon the minister's face. I say to him that if the speculation in the newspapers is correct, and if he does move to this other post in the cabinet, that of external affairs, I hope he will be more tactful and diplomatic in that post than he has been as Minister of Finance.

It may be that he is considering a bi-partisan policy and will take the Leader of the Opposition into his ranks and thus pave the way for the appearance of Premier Smallwood as leader of the Liberal party. This may sound amazing and imaginative but in politics nothing is impossible, especially with the Tories in office.

Another matter mentioned in the amendment to the amendment was the rise in interest rates and this is a very crucial question because these rates represent a hidden drain on the purchasing power of all the taxpayers in Canada. Increases which may at first appear to be quite small -one-tenth of one per cent, for example- amount to a great deal when they are accumulated, and the effect of these higher rates of interest on the purchasing power of individuals, municipalities and provinces is most serious. At the present time these rates are at usurious levels and they are tending to creep even higher.
Municipalities, provinces and individuals are finding themselves in a very difficult position because of the attitudes and actions of the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming)
The Budget-Mr. Howard and the present government. In fact, they are trapped. The municipalities, provinces and individuals are trapped in this interest rate by what one might classify as "Fleming's foolishness".

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Seriously, the Toronto Maple Leafs have been favourites of mine ever since I was a small child and first began listening to hockey games over the old crystal set.
When we come to talk about interest rates we can look back only a little while ago to that time when the Minister of Finance was gloating and rubbing his hands in glee over the decline in the rediscount rate on treasury bills. It was not long ago that he was asked questions about this. They are recorded in Hansard and if I have to refer to them for the exact words, I will. At that time the minister said the lowering of the rediscount rate on treasury bills was directly the result of the action of this government. He explained that it meant that inflation was curbed because interest rates were going down. He suggested that it meant the economy was recovering and that it marked the end of the tight money policy of the Liberals. He sat there and mustered together as large a smile as he is capable of producing and said these things with apparent open honesty. He attempted to take the credit saying it was the result of the efforts of his government that interest rates were lowered.
Following that we had the conversion loan which was designed, the minister said, to stabilize the money market. In this instance, I refer to page 4598 of Hansard of September 4, 1958 where my hon. friend who may be going to some other post in the cabinet is reported as having said:
I will say without fear of contradiction on the part of any responsible source in this country-
The minister took in a pretty wide territory, speaking for everyone in Canada. He continued:
-that the effect of the Canadian conversion loan has been to stabilize the market and in that way it has contributed not only to preventing a further

The Budget-Mr. Howard
rise in interest rates but in checking it and turning the tide in that respect. That is the effect of this issue.
At the end of August at about the time the conversion loan was to go into effect the rediscount rate was somewhere in the neighbourhood of 1.4 to 1.7 per cent. That was in the last part of August or the first week of September. Since that conversion loan took effect interest rates have climbed higher and higher and today they are at the highest point they have ever reached in the history of Canada. What does the Minister of Finance, silent Sam, do now? He keeps his mouth shut. He does not talk about that because it is embarrassing to the government to find out that today the rediscount rate stands at 4.86 per cent, an increase of 1.9 per cent over a week ago, as a direct result of the budget.
I observe that the minister shakes his head and denies that this was a result of the budget. The minister is at liberty to deny that. All I have to do is look back at the number of statements he has made since assuming that portfolio. He has been wrong so many times that it is obviously doubtful if we should pay any attention to the statements he makes at this time.
In the one instance he is only too eager to accept the credit, but in the other instance he keeps his mouth shut. I say to him that if this government is going to take the credit for those periods when the sun shines it also has to take full responsibility for those periods when it rains. Today was a beautiful summer-like day with high temperatures and it is a wonder that some hon. gentleman opposite did not rise in his place and make the statement that the weather has now been placed under the jurisdiction of the federal government.
This treasury bill rate reflects government policy as the Minister of Finance has told us so many times in the past. It is indeed a direct result of government action, attitudes and policies and represents a direct return to the situation that existed when the Liberals were in office, not a tight money policy but an even tighter money policy. My hon. friend shakes his head again. Perhaps he does not know what tight money is. Money is tight with me all the time and if interest rates go up much higher I, like some other hon. members of this house, may have to find a part-time job.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

It may well be that my employers, the constituents in Skeena, may decide to employ me full-time someday. That
is,	of course, a decision that they may take and there will not be much I can do about
it,	although I shall attempt to convince them that they have an excellent employee in me and should continue to employ me, which is a course followed by everyone in this house.
I should like to deal now with the effect of a financial policy of the government which has been mentioned by two or three hon. members, some in a derogatory way, some in a way that indicates they have not the foggiest idea what it is about and others in a partially sensible way in which they attempted to look at both sides of the picture.
The hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Keays) who preceded me in this debate mentioned what he thought was the effect of wage increases on the economy. The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Horner) in either the throne speech debate or in a speech on the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, I forget which, also used the same approach and drew the analogy that because wages go up the farm implement machinery industry has to increase the prices of farm machinery and therefore the hon. member blamed the wages of workingmen for the higher prices of the materials used by manufacturers in producing farm machinery and the resultant higher costs of farm machinery and equipment.
My friend the hon. member for Acadia may know something about farming but it is extremely obvious that he does not know a darn thing about the relationship of wages and trade unions to the general economy.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it ten o'clock and in the same breath announce that the score is still 1-0.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I may ask the Minister of Finance if it is proposed to go on tomorrow with the same debate?

subtopic: CHICAGO DIVERSION

speechtext:
NO. 184 Sir,
I have the honour on instructions from my government to refer to proposals for legislation in the United States of America concerning an increase in the diversion of water from lake Michigan through the Chicago drainage canal. It is noted that one proposal to this effect has been approved by the House of Representatives and will shortly be considered by the Senate. During a period of many years there have been numerous occasions on which the government of Canada has made representations to the government of the U.S.A. with respect to proposals concerning the diversion of water from lake Michigan out of the great lakes watershed at Chicago.
Many of these representations have been directed toward particular proposals then under discussion by U.S.A. authorities. Because of the importance of the question, the government of Canada believes it timely to re-examine the considerations which it regards as most important concerning any proposals for additional diversion of water from the great lakes watershed. Accordingly, in order that there may be no misunderstanding as to the views of the government of Canada,
I have been instructed to bring the following considerations to your attention.
Every diversion of water from the great lakes watershed at Chicago inevitably decreases the volume of water remaining in the basin for all purposes. The government of Canada is opposed to any action which will have the effect of reducing the volume of water in the great lakes basin. Careful inquiry has failed to reveal any sources of water in Canada which could be added to the present supplies of the basin to compensate for further withdrawals in the U.S.A. The government of Canada considers that many agreements and understandings between the U.S.A. and Canada would be broken if unilateral action were taken to divert additional water from the great lakes watershed at Chicago and directs attention to provisions of two treaties in particular
(a) The boundary waters treaty, 1909: The applicability of either art. II, para. 2 or art.
Ill of this treaty depends upon the interpretation of physical facts.
If lake Michigan physically flows into the boundary water lake Huron, art. II preserves

to Canada the right to object to such a diversion which would be productive of material injury to the navigation interests in Canadian waters.
If, as has been asserted by eminent U.S.A. jurists, art. III of the treaty applies, no further diversion shall be made except with the approval of the international joint commission.
(b) Niagara treaty, 1950: This treaty allocates water for scenic and power purposes. The amount of water which shall be available for these purposes is the total outflow from lake Erie. The specific inclusion of certain added waters in art. Ill of the treaty emphasizes the underlying assumption that existing supplies will continue unabated. In addition to these treaty provisions, there is a further agreement of far-reaching importance. Power development in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec is predicated upon agreed criteria for regulation of the flows of the St. Lawrence river. The order of approval of the international joint commission of October 29, 1952 as supplemented on July 2, 1956 and accepted by both our governments, forms the basis for the construction and operation of the hydroelectric power installations in the international section of the St. Lawrence river. Criterion (a) of this order of approval assumes a continuous diversion out of the great lakes basin limited to the present 3,100 cubic feet per second at Chicago.
Navigation and commercial interests depend upon the maintenance of the basis upon which channel enlargements have been designed in order that vessels of deep draught may proceed with full load to and from the ports of the upper great lakes. In this connection I would refer to the following matters:
(a)	The construction of the St. Lawrence seaway. Legislation in the two countries and the several exchanges of notes concerning the construction and operation of the seaway now just completed are based on the assumption and understanding that there will not be unilateral action repugnant to the purposes of the legislation. Withdrawal of water from the great lakes basin would materially affect the operation of the St. Lawrence seaway;
(b)	Dredging. By agreement contained in the various exchanges of notes between the two countries, profiles have been prepared for the excavation which has taken place or is about to take place in the International rapids section of the river, in the Amherstburg channel and in the St. Clair river. These agreements are based on the implied understanding

that material changes would not be made in the volume of water available for navigation;
(c) New channel. In an exchange of notes dated February 28, 1959, it has been agreed that a new channel should be constructed to eliminate the so-called southeast bend of the St. Clair river. The agreement by the government of Canada to this proposal was based on the understanding that there would be no artificial interference with the present supplies of water.
Because of the importance attached by the U.S.A. and Canada to the honouring of international undertakings in letter and in spirit, the government of Canada views with serious concern any possible impairment of agreements and undertakings relating to the great lakes basin. Furthermore, the alarms created by repeated proposals for diversion which inevitably disturb the people and industry of
Chicago Water Diversion Canada are a source of profound irritation to the relations between our two countries which we can ill afford.
I am instructed, therefore, to express the hope of the government of Canada that the U.S.A. will view this matter with equal concern and will be able to give satisfactory assurances that unilateral action will not be taken which would imperil the present regime of the waters in the great lakes basin and the status of the agreements and understandings to which I have referred.
Please accept, sir, the renewed assurances of my highest consideration.
A. D. P. Heeney
The Canadian Embassy,
Washington, D. C.
April 9, 1959.
